arXiv:2609.04056v1 [math.OC] 03 Sep 2026

Factor-parity Hall sets and controllability:
a classification of good and bad brackets

Karine Beauchard ††thanks: Univ Rennes, CNRS, IRMAR - UMR 6625, F-35000 Rennes, France    Frédéric Marbach ††thanks: DMA, École normale supérieure, Université PSL, CNRS, 75005 Paris, France
Abstract

We introduce a class of Hall sets, which we call factor-parity Hall sets, whose elements split into good and bad brackets. We prove that the good brackets can be steered simultaneously and arbitrarily in small time, which yields sufficient conditions for the small-time local controllability of control-affine systems. This positive result draws on constructions of Kawski, Agrachev–Gamkrelidze and Krastanov. Conversely, we prove that each bad bracket generates an obstruction to controllability, hence a family of necessary conditions.

1 Introduction

1.1 Small-time local controllability of control-affine systems

In this article, we consider multi-input control-affine systems of the form

x˙​(t)=f0​(x⁡(t))+u1​(t)​f1​(x⁡(t))+⋯+uq​(t)​fq​(x⁡(t))\dot{x}(t)=f_{0}(x(t))+u_{1}(t)f_{1}(x(t))+\dotsb+u_{q}(t)f_{q}(x(t)) (1.1)

where the state x⁡(t)x(t) belongs to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥1d\geq 1), u:[0,T]→ℝqu:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{q} is the control, f0,f1,…,fqf_{0},f_{1},\dotsc,f_{q} (q≥1q\geq 1) are real-analytic vector fields on a fixed open neighborhood Ω\Omega of 00, and we assume that f0​(0)=0f_{0}(0)=0.

For each T>0T>0, each u∈L1​((0,T),ℝq)u\in L^{1}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) and each x∘∈Ωx^{\circ}\in\Omega, the Cauchy problem (1.1) with initial condition x⁡(0)=x∘x(0)=x^{\circ} admits a unique maximal absolutely continuous solution. We will consider small enough data so that this solution is defined up to time TT.

In this article, we study the following standard notion of small-time local controllability of system (1.1) with controls small in L∞L^{\infty} (see e.g. [8, Definition 3.2] or STLCε in [14]).

Definition 1.1.

We say that (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC when, for all T,ρ>0T,\rho>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that, for any x∘,x∗∈ℝdx^{\circ},x^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with |x∘|+|x∗|≤δ\lvert x^{\circ}\rvert+\lvert x^{*}\rvert\leq\delta, there exists u∈L∞​((0,T),ℝq)u\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) with ∥u∥L∞≤ρ\lVert u\rVert_{L^{\infty}}\leq\rho such that the associated solution to (1.1) with initial condition x⁡(0)=x∘x(0)=x^{\circ} satisfies x⁡(T)=x∗x(T)=x^{*}.

1.2 Algebraic notations and Lie brackets

Let XX be an arbitrary set of unknowns. We denote by Br⁡(X)\Br(X) the free magma on XX, by ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X) the free Lie algebra over ℝ\mathbb{R} generated by XX, and by e the unique magma morphism Br⁡(X)→(ℒ⁡(X),[⋅,⋅])\Br(X)\to(\mathcal{L}(X),[\cdot,\cdot]) extending idX\operatorname{id}_{X}. In the sequel, implicitly, ℝ\mathbb{R} is the base field of all vector spaces, algebras, Lie algebras, etc. We refer to Section 2 or [4, Section 2.1] for more details on these standard objects.

In this paper, the notion of Hall set plays a central role. There are different conventions in the literature: one may decide to swap left and right factors, or swap the order, or both. We follow Viennot’s convention of [22] (also used in control theory by Sussmann [20]).

Definition 1.2 (Hall set).

A Hall set on XX is a totally ordered subset (ℬ,<)(\mathcal{B},<) of Br⁡(X)\Br(X) such that

  • •

    X⊂ℬX\subset\mathcal{B},

  • •

    for a,b∈Br⁡(X)a,b\in\Br(X), (a,b)∈ℬ(a,b)\in\mathcal{B} iff a,b∈ℬa,b\in\mathcal{B}, a<ba<b and either b∈Xb\in X or b=(b′,b′′)b=(b^{\prime},b^{\prime\prime}) with b′≤ab^{\prime}\leq a,

  • •

    for every a,b∈ℬa,b\in\mathcal{B} such that (a,b)∈ℬ(a,b)\in\mathcal{B}, one has a<(a,b)a<(a,b).

The main interest of Hall sets is that their images under e yield algebraic bases of ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X), called Hall bases, as proved in [22, Corollary 1.1, Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 1.1].

Proposition 1.3.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a Hall set on XX. Then e​(ℬ)\textnormal{{e}}(\mathcal{B}) is a basis of ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X).

Our controllability conditions will be expressed using the iterated Lie brackets of the vector fields involved in (1.1). We use the following convention and notation.

Definition 1.4 (Lie brackets of vector fields).

We endow the vector subspace Cω​(Ω,ℝd)C^{\omega}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) of real-analytic vector fields on Ω\Omega with a Lie algebra structure by setting [f,g]:=(D​g)​f−(D​f)​g[f,g]:=(Dg)f-(Df)g.

Definition 1.5 (Evaluation of Lie brackets).

Let X={X0,X1,…,Xq}X=\{X_{0},X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\}. For B∈ℒ⁡(X)B\in\mathcal{L}(X), we denote by fB∈Cω​(Ω,ℝd)f_{B}\in C^{\omega}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) the image of BB under the unique Lie algebra homomorphism ℒ⁡(X)→Cω​(Ω,ℝd)\mathcal{L}(X)\to C^{\omega}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) mapping XiX_{i} to fif_{i}. For b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X), we write fb:=fe​(b)f_{b}:=f_{\textnormal{{e}}(b)}, so that fXi=fif_{X_{i}}=f_{i} and f(a,b)=[fa,fb]f_{(a,b)}=[f_{a},f_{b}] for a,b∈Br⁡(X)a,b\in\Br(X). Finally, fb​(0)∈ℝdf_{b}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes its value at x=0x=0.

1.3 Statement of the main results

In Section 2, we define a class of Hall sets, which we call factor-parity Hall sets. Let us already mention that, starting from a partition X=Xgood⊔XbadX=X_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup X_{\mathrm{bad}} of the alphabet XX, a factor-parity Hall set ℬ\mathcal{B} on XX comes with a partition into good and bad brackets of the form ℬ=ℬgood⊔ℬbad\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}.

We consider a multi-input control-affine system of the form (1.1). We assume that it satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition:

Lie⁡(f0,f1,…,fq)​(0)=ℝd.\operatorname{Lie}(f_{0},f_{1},\dotsc,f_{q})(0)=\mathbb{R}^{d}. (1.2)

In the following statements, ℬ\mathcal{B} is a factor-parity Hall set on X=Xgood⊔XbadX=X_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup X_{\mathrm{bad}} where Xgood={X1,…,Xq}X_{\mathrm{good}}=\{X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\} and Xbad={X0}X_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{X_{0}\}. Our main results are the following conditions.

Theorem 1.6 (Sufficient condition).

If, for all b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, fb​(0)=0f_{b}(0)=0, then (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC.

Theorem 1.7 (Necessary condition).

Assume that there exists b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} such that

fb​(0)∉span⁡{fa​(0)∣a∈ℬgood}f_{b}(0)\notin\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid a\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\} (1.3)

and

∀a∈ℬbad∖{b},fa​(0)=0.\forall a\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\setminus\{b\},\quad f_{a}(0)=0. (1.4)

Then (1.1) is not L∞L^{\infty}-STLC.

The complementarity between Theorems 1.6 and 1.7 settles an open question in control theory concerning the classification of brackets (see [14, Section 4]). Heuristically, they can be rephrased as follows:

  • •

    if all bad brackets vanish, then the system is controllable;

  • •

    if all but one bad brackets vanish, and this single bad bracket is not compensated, then the system is not controllable.

1.3.1 Relaxed sufficient condition

The condition that all bad brackets vanish is unnecessarily strong. Using rescaled controls of the form ε1−θu(⋅/εθ)\varepsilon^{1-\theta}u(\cdot/\varepsilon^{\theta}) as in [21], one easily obtains the following relaxed version where one allows bad brackets to be compensated by good ones of lower weight. For a given b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X) and θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), set

ωθ​(b):=θ​n0​(b)+(n1​(b)+⋯+nq​(b))\omega_{\theta}(b):=\theta n_{0}(b)+(n_{1}(b)+\dotsb+n_{q}(b)) (1.5)

where ni​(b)n_{i}(b) denotes the number of occurrences of the letter XiX_{i} in bb.

We will prove the following better sufficient condition.

Theorem 1.8.

Assume that there exists θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) such that, for all b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}},

fb(0)∈span{fa(0)∣a∈ℬgood,ωθ(a)<ωθ(b)}.f_{b}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid a\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}},\ \omega_{\theta}(a)<\omega_{\theta}(b)\}. (1.6)

Then (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC.

1.3.2 Relaxed necessary condition

The condition that all bad brackets except the considered one vanish is probably too stringent and might be somewhat relaxed.

However, there is an underlying difficulty which cannot be overlooked concerning the possibility to obtain L∞L^{\infty}-STLC through the competition of bad brackets. This possibility had already been identified in [14, Section 5]. We introduced the following example, with a scalar-input control, in [6, Proposition 1.21]:

{x˙1=u,x˙2=x1,x˙3=x2,x˙4=x12​x32−λ​x24.\begin{cases}\dot{x}_{1}=u,\\ \dot{x}_{2}=x_{1},\\ \dot{x}_{3}=x_{2},\\ \dot{x}_{4}=x_{1}^{2}x_{3}^{2}-\lambda x_{2}^{4}.\end{cases} (1.7)

It is proved in [6, Section 6] that there exists λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0 such that, for all λ>λ∗\lambda>\lambda^{*}, this system is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC. Let M1:=(X1,X0)M_{1}:=(X_{1},X_{0}), M2:=(M1,X0)M_{2}:=(M_{1},X_{0}), M3:=(M2,X0)M_{3}:=(M_{2},X_{0}), Q1,3,3:=adM22​adX12⁡(X0)Q_{1,3,3}:=\ad_{M_{2}}^{2}\ad_{X_{1}}^{2}(X_{0}) and Q2,2,2:=adM14⁡(X0)Q_{2,2,2}:=\ad_{M_{1}}^{4}(X_{0}). Any factor-parity Hall set contains all these brackets, the first 3 being good, and the last two bad. System (1.7) is controllable thanks to a competition between these two bad quartic brackets. Hence, a condition of the form (1.3) is insufficient to deny STLC. It is mandatory to add some kind of assumption on the other bad brackets. As a first step, we choose here the blunt formulation (1.4).

1.4 Comparison with known results

1.4.1 Sufficient conditions

We start with a famous sufficient condition due to Sussmann [21]. Recalling the notation ni​(b)n_{i}(b) for the number of occurrences of the letter XiX_{i} in bb, we define a set of “Sussmann-bad” brackets as follows:

Sbad:={b∈Br⁡(X)∣n0​(b)​ is odd and ​ni​(b)​ is even for all ​1≤i≤q}.S_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\{b\in\Br(X)\mid n_{0}(b)\text{ is odd and }n_{i}(b)\text{ is even for all }1\leq i\leq q\}. (1.8)

Sussmann proved the following result in [21].

Theorem 1.9.

Assume that {f0,f1,…,fq}\left\{f_{0},f_{1},\dotsc,f_{q}\right\} satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition (1.2). Assume that there exists θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) such that, for the weight (1.5), for all b∈Sbadb\in S_{\mathrm{bad}},

fb(0)∈span{fa(0)∣a∈Br(X),ωθ(a)<ωθ(b)}.f_{b}(0)\in\operatorname{span}\left\{f_{a}(0)\mid a\in\Br(X),\ \omega_{\theta}(a)<\omega_{\theta}(b)\right\}. (1.9)

Then system (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC.

Proof.

See [21, Section 7.3] choosing Λ0\Lambda_{0} to be the group of automorphisms generated only by the σi\sigma_{i} (not the π\pi, π~\tilde{\pi}). ∎

Sussmann’s sufficient condition exploits the input symmetries ui↦−uiu_{i}\mapsto-u_{i} (which dates back to the Hermes sufficient condition [11, 19]) and u↦uˇu\mapsto\check{u} (time reversal, which had been observed in particular cases by Stefani in [18]). The brackets b∈Sbadb\in S_{\mathrm{bad}} are the ones whose coordinates are invariant under these natural substitutions. Our sufficient condition Theorem 1.8 requires the compensation of far fewer brackets (see Section A.3 for a detailed comparison).

In [13], Kawski observed that some brackets of SbadS_{\mathrm{bad}} could lead to controllable systems. His proof introduced a new argument, which can be seen as the repetition of a given control pattern concatenated multiple times with itself. This idea started a fruitful line of work, including [1] by Agrachev and Gamkrelidze, [15] by Krastanov, and the current work, which pushes the approach recursively, encoding it into a Hall set.

When expressed in a Hall set, our sufficient conditions Theorems 1.6 and 1.8 require the compensation of fewer bad brackets than Agrachev–Gamkrelidze or Krastanov (see Section A.4 for a detailed comparison). Nevertheless, the core proof mechanism is similar, and our sufficient condition can be seen as an automatically-expanded version of their conditions.

1.4.2 Necessary conditions

Comparatively, less attention had been devoted to the derivation of necessary conditions for STLC, and one only knew obstructions related to very specific brackets or small families of brackets. Some of these obstructions to controllability have also been observed for PDEs (see the survey [7]).

Scalar-input case q=1q=1.

Most known necessary conditions concern the scalar-input case q=1q=1. Let us survey this case. We fix some notation. Let M0:=X1M_{0}:=X_{1} and Mν+1:=(Mν,X0)M_{\nu+1}:=(M_{\nu},X_{0}) for ν≥0\nu\geq 0.

Historically, the first obstruction to controllability discovered is the one associated with the bad bracket W1:=(X1,(X1,X0))=adX12⁡(X0)=adM02⁡(X0)W_{1}:=(X_{1},(X_{1},X_{0}))=\ad_{X_{1}}^{2}(X_{0})=\ad_{M_{0}}^{2}(X_{0}). It is associated with the following necessary condition for L∞L^{\infty}-STLC:

fW1​(0)∈span⁡{fa​(0)∣n1​(a)=1}.f_{W_{1}}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid n_{1}(a)=1\}. (1.10)

See [19, Proposition 6.3] for the historical proof.

A first generalization of this condition was proved by Stefani in [18]. She proved that, if (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC, then, for all k∈ℕ∗k\in\mathbb{N}^{*},

fadX12​k⁡(X0)​(0)∈span⁡{fa​(0)∣n1​(a)<2​k}.f_{\ad^{2k}_{X_{1}}(X_{0})}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid n_{1}(a)<2k\}. (1.11)

In [13], Kawski proved that, if (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC, then, for W2:=adM12⁡(X0)W_{2}:=\ad_{M_{1}}^{2}(X_{0}) and P=adX13⁡(X0)P=\ad_{X_{1}}^{3}(X_{0}),

fW2​(0)∈span⁡{fa​(0)∣n1​(a)=1​ or ​a=adX0ν​adX13⁡(X0)}.f_{W_{2}}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid n_{1}(a)=1\text{ or }a=\ad_{X_{0}}^{\nu}\ad_{X_{1}}^{3}(X_{0})\}. (1.12)

We generalized this condition by proving in [5, Theorem 1.11] the following necessary condition for L∞L^{\infty}-STLC, conjectured by Kawski in [12, p. 63], for Wk:=adMk−12⁡(X0)W_{k}:=\ad_{M_{k-1}}^{2}(X_{0}),

fWk​(0)∈span⁡{fa​(0)∣n1​(a)=1​ or ​2<n1​(a)<2​k}.f_{W_{k}}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid n_{1}(a)=1\text{ or }2<n_{1}(a)<2k\}. (1.13)

In [5, Section 3], we also constructed a Hall set ℬ⋆\mathcal{B}^{\star} for which we proved in [5, Theorem 1.14] the following necessary condition for L∞L^{\infty}-STLC, with P=adX13⁡(X0)P=\ad_{X_{1}}^{3}(X_{0}),

fadP2⁡(X0)(0)∈span{fa(0)∣a∈ℬ⋆,n1(a)≤7 and a≠adP2(X0)}.f_{\ad^{2}_{P}(X_{0})}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid a\in\mathcal{B}^{\star},\ n_{1}(a)\leq 7\text{ and }a\neq\ad_{P}^{2}(X_{0})\}. (1.14)

For the same basis ℬ⋆\mathcal{B}^{\star}, we proved in [6, Section 7.1] many necessary conditions for STLC based on quartic brackets, i.e. brackets with n1=4n_{1}=4. For example, we proved that, with Qj,k,k:=adMk−12​adMj−12⁡(X0)Q_{j,k,k}:=\ad_{M_{k-1}}^{2}\ad_{M_{j-1}}^{2}(X_{0}) for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, and k≤2​jk\leq 2j, a necessary condition for L∞L^{\infty}-STLC is that

fQj,k,k(0)∈span{fa(0)∣a∈ℬ⋆,n1(a)≤2j+2k−1, and a≠Qj,k,k}.f_{Q_{j,k,k}}(0)\in\vect\{f_{a}(0)\mid a\in\mathcal{B}^{\star},\ n_{1}(a)\leq 2j+2k-1,\text{ and }a\neq Q_{j,k,k}\}. (1.15)

Note that all the brackets above belong to all Hall sets of the factor-parity class, and are all indeed classified as bad by these Hall sets.

Multi-input case q>1q>1.

Generally speaking, it is much harder to prove obstructions in the multi-input case q>1q>1 and the conditions are harder to state. Let us mention two possible approaches. In [10], the authors explore, when q=2q=2 and f2​(0)=0f_{2}(0)=0, obstructions caused by the brackets W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} above, by enlarging the compensating sets. In [9], the author explores obstructions linked with the simultaneous presence of the brackets adXi2⁡(X0)\ad_{X_{i}}^{2}(X_{0}) for i=1,…,qi=1,\dotsc,q.

Comparison.

A strong advantage of our result Theorem 1.7 is that we have a classification of the full Hall set on {X0,X1,…,Xq}\{X_{0},X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\}, giving a general framework to identify bad brackets. However, the non-compensation assumption (1.3) is very far from sharp.

1.4.3 Classification results

In [6, Section 5], we discussed the classification problem, dating back to [14, Section 4]. Using the Hall set ℬ⋆\mathcal{B}^{\star} introduced in [5, Section 3], we proved that it could classify (in some precise sense) the brackets of Br⁡(X)\Br(X) containing up to 4 occurrences of X1X_{1}. The main strength of our current work is to produce such a classification for a full Hall set.

1.5 Organization of the paper

In Section 2, we give definitions building up to the notion of factor-parity Hall set. In Section 3, we prove the sufficient conditions of Theorems 1.6 and 1.8. In Sections 4 and 5, we prove the necessary condition of Theorem 1.7.

2 Definitions

Throughout this section, XX is an arbitrary set of unknowns.

2.1 Free magma and factorization

Recall that we denote by Br⁡(X)\Br(X) the free magma on XX. We will use the following associated notions.

For b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X), |b||b| denotes the length of bb. If |b|>1|b|>1, bb can be written in a unique way as b=(b′,b′′)b=(b^{\prime},b^{\prime\prime}), with b′,b′′∈Br⁡(X)b^{\prime},b^{\prime\prime}\in\Br(X). We use the notations λ⁡(b)=b′\lambda(b)=b^{\prime} and μ⁡(b)=b′′\mu(b)=b^{\prime\prime}, which define maps λ,μ:Br⁡(X)∖X→Br⁡(X)\lambda,\mu:\Br(X)\setminus X\to\Br(X). We also denote by degX⁡(b)∈ℕ(X)\deg_{X}(b)\in\mathbb{N}^{(X)} the multidegree of bb, supp⁡degX⁡(b)⊂X\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(b)\subset X the set of letters occurring in bb and degx⁡(b)∈ℕ\deg_{x}(b)\in\mathbb{N} the number of occurrences of the letter xx in bb. For a∈Br⁡(X)a\in\Br(X), let ada:Br⁡(X)→Br⁡(X)\ad_{a}:\Br(X)\to\Br(X) be the map defined by ada⁡(b):=(a,b)\ad_{a}(b):=(a,b).

For example, when X={X0,X1,X2}X=\{X_{0},X_{1},X_{2}\}, a=adX12⁡(X0)=(X1,(X1,X0))∈Br⁡(X)a=\ad_{X_{1}}^{2}(X_{0})=(X_{1},(X_{1},X_{0}))\in\Br(X) satisfies |a|=3|a|=3, λ⁡(a)=X1\lambda(a)=X_{1}, μ⁡(a)=(X1,X0)\mu(a)=(X_{1},X_{0}) and degX(a)={X0↦1,X1↦2,X2↦0}\deg_{X}(a)=\{X_{0}\mapsto 1,X_{1}\mapsto 2,X_{2}\mapsto 0\} so that supp⁡degX⁡(a)={X0,X1}\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(a)=\{X_{0},X_{1}\} and degX1⁡(a)=2\deg_{X_{1}}(a)=2.

Definition 2.1 (Factors).

For b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X), we define by induction on length its factors as

Fac⁡(b):={∅,if ​b∈X,{a}∪Fac⁡(c),if ​b=(a,c).\operatorname{Fac}(b):=\begin{cases}\varnothing,&\text{if }b\in X,\\ \{a\}\cup\operatorname{Fac}(c),&\text{if }b=(a,c).\end{cases} (2.1)

For B⊂Br⁡(X)B\subset\Br(X), we write Fac⁡(B):=⋃b∈BFac⁡(b)\operatorname{Fac}(B):=\bigcup_{b\in B}\operatorname{Fac}(b) and we call BB factor-stable when Fac⁡(B)⊂B\operatorname{Fac}(B)\subset B.

Definition 2.2 (Factor closure).

Given B⊂Br⁡(X)B\subset\Br(X), let Fac+⁡(B)\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(B) denote the smallest factor-stable subset of Br⁡(X)\Br(X) containing Fac⁡(B)\operatorname{Fac}(B). We also let Fac∗⁡(B):=B∪Fac+⁡(B)\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(B):=B\cup\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(B). For a singleton, Fac+⁡(b):=Fac+⁡({b})\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(b):=\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(\{b\}) and Fac∗⁡(b):=Fac∗⁡({b})\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b):=\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(\{b\}).

Lemma 2.3.

If S,E⊂Br⁡(X)S,E\subset\Br(X) are such that SS is factor-stable and Fac⁡(E)⊂S\operatorname{Fac}(E)\subset S, then Fac+⁡(E)⊂S\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(E)\subset S.

Lemma 2.4 (Factorization and seed).

For b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X), there exists a unique r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}, m1,…,mr≥1m_{1},\dotsc,m_{r}\geq 1, a1,…,ar∈Br⁡(X)a_{1},\dotsc,a_{r}\in\Br(X) with aj≠aj+1a_{j}\neq a_{j+1} for 1≤j<r1\leq j<r, and Xi∈XX_{i}\in X such that

b=adarmr​⋯​ada1m1⁡(Xi).b=\ad_{a_{r}}^{m_{r}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(X_{i}). (2.2)

We call this expression of bb its factorization, and one has

Fac⁡(b)={a1,…,ar}andFac∗⁡(b)={b}∪⋃1≤j≤rFac∗⁡(aj).\operatorname{Fac}(b)=\{a_{1},\dotsc,a_{r}\}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)=\{b\}\cup\bigcup_{1\leq j\leq r}\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(a_{j}). (2.3)

We call XiX_{i} the seed of bb and we use the notation seed⁡(b):=Xi∈X\operatorname{seed}(b):=X_{i}\in X.

When b∈Xb\in X, its factorization is just b=Xib=X_{i}, so r=0r=0, Fac⁡(b)=∅\operatorname{Fac}(b)=\varnothing and seed⁡(b)=b\operatorname{seed}(b)=b.

2.2 Factorization in Hall sets

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a Hall set on XX.

Lemma 2.5 (Factorization in a Hall set).

For all b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}, the factors of bb given in (2.2) belong to ℬ\mathcal{B} and satisfy a1<⋯<ar<ba_{1}<\dotsb<a_{r}<b and a1<seed⁡(b)a_{1}<\operatorname{seed}(b).

Proof.

The fact that ai∈ℬa_{i}\in\mathcal{B} and the inequality chain a1<⋯<ara_{1}<\dotsb<a_{r} follow from the second Hall axiom. By the third Hall axiom, ar<ba_{r}<b. Since the innermost bracket (a1,seed⁡(b))∈ℬ(a_{1},\operatorname{seed}(b))\in\mathcal{B}, a1<seed⁡(b)a_{1}<\operatorname{seed}(b) by the second Hall axiom. ∎

Lemma 2.6.

Let p∈ℬp\in\mathcal{B}. Then ℬ<p:={b∈ℬ∣b<p}\mathcal{B}_{<p}:=\{b\in\mathcal{B}\mid b<p\} is factor-stable.

Proof.

Let b∈ℬ<pb\in\mathcal{B}_{<p} and a∈Fac⁡(b)a\in\operatorname{Fac}(b). By Lemma 2.5, a<ba<b. Hence a<pa<p and a∈ℬ<pa\in\mathcal{B}_{<p}. ∎

Lemma 2.7 (Minimum of the factor closure).

Let b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}. Then

  1. (i)

    supp⁡degX⁡(a)⊂supp⁡degX⁡(b)\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(a)\subset\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(b) for every a∈Fac∗⁡(b)a\in\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b);

  2. (ii)

    min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)∈X\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\in X;

  3. (iii)

    min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)=min⁡supp​degX⁡(b)\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)=\min\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(b).

Proof.

(i) By additivity of the multidegree, degx⁡(a)≤degx⁡(b)\deg_{x}(a)\leq\deg_{x}(b) for any x∈Xx\in X.

(ii) By contradiction, assume that x:=min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)x:=\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b) is not a letter. Then Fac⁡(x)≠∅\operatorname{Fac}(x)\neq\varnothing. Let a∈Fac⁡(x)a\in\operatorname{Fac}(x). Since Fac∗⁡(b)\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b) is factor-stable, a∈Fac∗⁡(b)a\in\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b). By Lemma 2.5, a<xa<x, a contradiction.

(iii) Proceed by induction on |b|\lvert b\rvert, the case b∈Xb\in X being trivial. Let bb be as in (2.2). Since min⁡Fac∗⁡(aj)≤aj<b\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(a_{j})\leq a_{j}<b by Lemma 2.5, (2.3) gives

min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)=minj​min​Fac∗⁡(aj)=minj⁡min⁡supp​degX⁡(aj),\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)=\min_{j}\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(a_{j})=\min_{j}\min\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(a_{j}), (2.4)

the second equality by the induction assumption.

By Lemma 2.5, a1<seed⁡(b)a_{1}<\operatorname{seed}(b), whence min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)≤a1<seed⁡(b)\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\leq a_{1}<\operatorname{seed}(b). Therefore

min⁡supp​degX⁡(b)=min⁡({seed⁡(b)}∪⋃jsupp⁡degX⁡(aj))=minj⁡min⁡supp​degX⁡(aj),\min\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(b)=\min\Bigl(\{\operatorname{seed}(b)\}\cup\bigcup_{j}\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(a_{j})\Bigr)=\min_{j}\min\operatorname{supp}\deg_{X}(a_{j}), (2.5)

which concludes the proof. ∎

2.3 Expansion in a basis given by a Hall set

Definition 2.8 (Support).

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a Hall set on XX. For z∈ℒ⁡(X)z\in\mathcal{L}(X) and b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}, we write ⟨z,b⟩ℬ\langle z,b\rangle_{\mathcal{B}} for the coordinate of zz along bb in the basis e​(ℬ)\textnormal{{e}}(\mathcal{B}). We define

suppℬ⁡(z):={b∈ℬ∣⟨z,b⟩ℬ≠0}.\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}(z):=\left\{b\in\mathcal{B}\mid\langle z,b\rangle_{\mathcal{B}}\neq 0\right\}. (2.6)

For a subset V⊂ℒ⁡(X)V\subset\mathcal{L}(X), we write suppℬ⁡(V):=⋃z∈Vsuppℬ⁡(z)\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}(V):=\bigcup_{z\in V}\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}(z).

The following structural property (proved in [3, Theorem 2.1]) follows from the classical recursive rewriting algorithm on Hall sets, described for example in [3, Section 2.1] or [17, Section 9].

Lemma 2.9.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a Hall set on XX and a<b∈ℬa<b\in\mathcal{B}. Then, either (a,b)∈ℬ(a,b)\in\mathcal{B}, or all elements c∈suppℬ⁡[a,b]c\in\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}[a,b] satisfy λ⁡(c)>a\lambda(c)>a. In both cases, for all c∈suppℬ⁡[a,b]c\in\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}[a,b], λ⁡(c)≥a\lambda(c)\geq a.

2.4 Hall order

As in [3, Section 1.4.2], one can construct Hall sets from given orders on subsets of Br⁡(X)\Br(X).

Definition 2.10.

We say that H⊂Br⁡(X)H\subset\Br(X) is λ\lambda-stable when, for all b∈H∖Xb\in H\setminus X, λ⁡(b)∈H\lambda(b)\in H.

Definition 2.11.

Let HH be a λ\lambda-stable subset of Br⁡(X)\Br(X). We say that << is a Hall order on HH when it is a total order such that, for all b∈H∖Xb\in H\setminus X, one has λ⁡(b)<b\lambda(b)<b.

Lemma 2.12.

Let HH be a λ\lambda-stable subset of Br⁡(X)\Br(X) with X⊂HX\subset H, endowed with a Hall order << such that, for all a<b∈Ha<b\in H, one has (a,b)∈H(a,b)\in H. There exists a unique Hall set ℬ⊂H\mathcal{B}\subset H over XX associated with this order.

Proof.

We show by induction that, for each ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, the set ℬℓ\mathcal{B}_{\ell} of elements of length ℓ\ell of ℬ\mathcal{B} is uniquely determined by the Hall axioms and the given order. By the first item of Definition 1.2, ℬ1=X\mathcal{B}_{1}=X. Then, for ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, by the second item of Definition 1.2,

ℬℓ={(a,b)∣a∈ℬℓ−1,b∈ℬ1,a<b}∪⋃1≤j≤ℓ−2{(a,b)∣a∈ℬj,b∈ℬℓ−j,λ(b)≤a<b}.\mathcal{B}_{\ell}=\{(a,b)\mid a\in\mathcal{B}_{\ell-1},b\in\mathcal{B}_{1},a<b\}\cup\bigcup_{1\leq j\leq\ell-2}\{(a,b)\mid a\in\mathcal{B}_{j},b\in\mathcal{B}_{\ell-j},\lambda(b)\leq a<b\}. (2.7)

The assumption that << is a Hall order yields the third item of Definition 1.2. ∎

2.5 Dichotomic Hall set

For our applications, it is helpful to construct Hall sets in which all “bad” brackets are ordered after all “good” brackets. Given a set A⊂Br⁡(X)A\subset\Br(X) of brackets identified as potentially bad, we prove the existence of such a Hall set. We define (A,A):={(a,b)∣a,b∈A}⊂Br(X)(A,A):=\{(a,b)\mid a,b\in A\}\subset\Br(X).

Proposition 2.13.

Let A⊂Br⁡(X)A\subset\Br(X) such that (A,A)⊂A(A,A)\subset A. Let ≺\prec be a Hall order on Br⁡(X)\Br(X). There exists a unique Hall set (ℬ,<)(\mathcal{B},<) such that, for all a,b∈ℬa,b\in\mathcal{B}, a<ba<b if and only if

  1. (i)

    either a∉Aa\notin A and b∈Ab\in A,

  2. (ii)

    or both a,b∈Aa,b\in A (or both a,b∉Aa,b\notin A) and a≺ba\prec b.

Proof.

Let HH be the subset of Br⁡(X)\Br(X) whose elements are the b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X) such that, for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that λk​(b)∉X\lambda^{k}(b)\notin X and λk+1​(b)∈A\lambda^{k+1}(b)\in A, one has μ​λk​(b)∈A\mu\lambda^{k}(b)\in A. Then HH is a λ\lambda-stable subset of Br⁡(X)\Br(X) with X⊂HX\subset H. We endow HH with a total order by setting a<ba<b if and only if (i) or (ii) holds.

Step 1: We prove that << is a Hall order on HH. Let b∈H∖Xb\in H\setminus X. Since ≺\prec is a Hall order, λ⁡(b)≺b\lambda(b)\prec b. If λ⁡(b)∉A\lambda(b)\notin A and b∈Ab\in A, then λ⁡(b)<b\lambda(b)<b by (i). If λ⁡(b)∉A\lambda(b)\notin A and b∉Ab\notin A, then λ⁡(b)<b\lambda(b)<b by (ii). If λ⁡(b)∈A\lambda(b)\in A then μ⁡(b)∈A\mu(b)\in A because b∈Hb\in H, thus b∈(A,A)⊂Ab\in(A,A)\subset A and λ⁡(b)<b\lambda(b)<b by (ii).

Step 2: We prove that, for all a<c∈Ha<c\in H, (a,c)∈H(a,c)\in H. Let a<c∈Ha<c\in H and b=(a,c)b=(a,c). We want to prove that for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that λk​(b)∉X\lambda^{k}(b)\notin X and λk+1​(b)∈A\lambda^{k+1}(b)\in A, one has μ​λk​(b)∈A\mu\lambda^{k}(b)\in A. This holds for k≥1k\geq 1 because a∈Ha\in H. It also holds for k=0k=0: indeed, if a∈Aa\in A then c∈Ac\in A by (i) because a<ca<c.

Step 3: Conclusion. The existence and uniqueness follow by Lemma 2.12.

Indeed, any Hall set satisfying (i) and (ii) must be included in HH. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be such a Hall set, b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that λk​(b)∉X\lambda^{k}(b)\notin X and λk+1​(b)∈A\lambda^{k+1}(b)\in A. Since λk​(b)∈ℬ\lambda^{k}(b)\in\mathcal{B}, by the second Hall axiom, λk+1​(b)<μ​λk​(b)\lambda^{k+1}(b)<\mu\lambda^{k}(b). By (i), μ​λk​(b)∈A\mu\lambda^{k}(b)\in A. So b∈Hb\in H. ∎

Proposition 2.14.

Let A⊂Br⁡(X)A\subset\Br(X) such that (A,A)⊂A(A,A)\subset A. Let ≺\prec be a Hall order on Br⁡(X)\Br(X). Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the Hall set given by Proposition 2.13. Define ℬbad:=ℬ∩A\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\mathcal{B}\cap A and ℬgood:=ℬ∖A\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}:=\mathcal{B}\setminus A. Then

  • •

    ℬgood<ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, i.e. a<ba<b for all a∈ℬgooda\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} and b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}},

  • •

    ℬgood\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} is factor-stable,

  • •

    if a,b∈ℬbada,b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, then suppℬ⁡[a,b]⊂ℬbad\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}[a,b]\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}.

Proof.

Let us prove each claim.

  • •

    The fact that ℬgood<ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} is a mere rewriting of item (i).

  • •

    Let b∈ℬgoodb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}. Write its factorization (2.2). By Lemma 2.5, a1<⋯<ar<ba_{1}<\dotsb<a_{r}<b. Since b∈ℬgoodb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}, by the first item, a1,…,ar∈ℬgooda_{1},\dotsc,a_{r}\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}.

    Let a,b∈ℬbada,b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} and c∈suppℬ⁡[a,b]c\in\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}[a,b]. By Lemma 2.9, λ⁡(c)≥min⁡(a,b)\lambda(c)\geq\min(a,b). By the third Hall set axiom of Definition 1.2, c>λ⁡(c)c>\lambda(c). By the first item, c∈ℬbadc\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}. ∎

2.6 Factor-parity Hall sets

Motivated by the analysis of the positivity properties of coordinates of the second kind (see Section 2.7), we introduce the following family of dichotomic Hall sets. We start from a partition

X=Xgood⊔Xbad.X=X_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup X_{\mathrm{bad}}. (2.8)
Definition 2.15 (Factor-parity Hall set).

We say that a Hall set ℬ\mathcal{B} over XX is of the factor-parity class for (2.8) when it splits as ℬ=ℬgood⊔ℬbad\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} with

  • •

    ℬgood<ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}};

  • •

    for every b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}, with the notation of (2.2),

    b∈ℬgood⇔Fac⁡(b)⊂ℬgood​ and ​(seed⁡(b)∈Xgood​ or ​mj​ odd for some ​j).b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\iff\operatorname{Fac}(b)\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\text{ and }\bigl(\operatorname{seed}(b)\in X_{\mathrm{good}}\text{ or }m_{j}\text{ odd for some }j\bigr). (2.9)
Remark 2.16.

Applying (2.9) to letters gives X∩ℬgood=XgoodX\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}=X_{\mathrm{good}} and X∩ℬbad=XbadX\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}=X_{\mathrm{bad}}.

Proposition 2.17 (Existence).

Let (2.8) be a partition of XX and ≺\prec be a Hall order on Br⁡(X)\Br(X). There exists a unique factor-parity Hall set (ℬ,<)(\mathcal{B},<) on XX such that for all a,b∈ℬgooda,b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} (or both in ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}), a<ba<b if and only if a≺ba\prec b.

Proof.

We define a subset H⊂Br⁡(X)H\subset\Br(X) by induction on length as follows. For b∈Br⁡(X)b\in\Br(X), writing its factorization as in (2.2), declare that

b∈H⟺a1,…,ar∈Hand(seed(b)∈Xgood)∨(∃j such that mj is odd).b\in H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_{1},\dotsc,a_{r}\in H\quad\text{and}\quad(\operatorname{seed}(b)\in X_{\mathrm{good}})\lor(\exists j\text{ such that }m_{j}\text{ is odd}). (2.10)

Set A:=Br⁡(X)∖HA:=\Br(X)\setminus H. If b=(a,c)∈(A,A)b=(a,c)\in(A,A) then a∈Fac⁡(b)a\in\operatorname{Fac}(b) and a∉Ha\notin H, so b∉Hb\notin H by (2.10). Hence (A,A)⊂A(A,A)\subset A. Let (ℬ,<)(\mathcal{B},<) be the Hall set given by Propositions 2.13 and 2.14. Let ℬgood:=ℬ∖A\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}:=\mathcal{B}\setminus A and ℬbad:=ℬ∩A\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\mathcal{B}\cap A. Since ℬgood=ℬ∩H\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}=\mathcal{B}\cap H, (2.10) yields (2.9). ∎

Corollary 2.18.

There exists a factor-parity Hall set for any partition (2.8).

Proof.

It suffices to choose an arbitrary Hall order on Br⁡(X)\Br(X) and apply Proposition 2.17. ∎

Its solution starting from the origin is the family (ξb​(t,u))b∈H(\xi_{b}(t,u))_{b\in H}.

When ΣH\Sigma_{H} is written as a control-affine system of the form (1.1), one has the canonical identity (see [2, Proposition 4.25]):

∀b∈ℬ,fb​(0)={∂xbif ​b∈H,0otherwise.\forall b\in\mathcal{B},\quad f_{b}(0)=\begin{cases}\partial_{x_{b}}&\text{if }b\in H,\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (2.17)

3 Proof of the sufficient condition

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a factor-parity Hall set on X={X0,X1,…,Xq}X=\{X_{0},X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\} with Xgood={X1,…,Xq}X_{\mathrm{good}}=\{X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\} and Xbad={X0}X_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{X_{0}\}. We prove Theorem 1.8 (which of course implies Theorem 1.6).

By classical arguments, it suffices to prove the following result.

Theorem 3.1.

Let G⊂ℬgoodG\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} be finite and factor-stable. Then the canonical system ΣG\Sigma_{G} of Definition 2.24 is small-time globally controllable. More precisely, for all T>0T>0 and x∘,x∗∈ℝGx^{\circ},x^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{G}, there exists u∈L∞​((0,T),ℝq)u\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that the associated solution to (2.16) satisfies x⁡(T,u,x∘)=x∗x(T;u,x^{\circ})=x^{*}.

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

We assumed that (1.1) satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition (1.2). Since bad brackets are compensated by assumption (1.6), one has span⁡{fb​(0)∣b∈ℬgood}=ℝd\vect\{f_{b}(0)\mid b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. Hence there exists a finite subset G⊂ℬgoodG\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} such that span⁡{fb​(0)∣b∈G}=ℝd\vect\{f_{b}(0)\mid b\in G\}=\mathbb{R}^{d} and, for all b∈ℬ∖Gb\in\mathcal{B}\setminus G, the compensation (1.6) holds. By (2.9), ℬgood\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} is factor-stable, so, up to replacing GG with Fac∗⁡(G)\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(G), we can assume that GG is both finite and factor-stable. By Theorem 3.1, ΣG\Sigma_{G} is small-time globally controllable. In particular, it admits a dual family in the sense of [6, Section A.2]. Thus, using the classical Sussmann control rescaling as in [6, Theorem A.14], we conclude that (1.1) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC. ∎

In this section, we therefore focus on proving Theorem 3.1. We recall the following classical result from control theory concerning normal accessibility.

Proposition 3.2.

Assume that {f0,f1,…,fq}\{f_{0},f_{1},\dotsc,f_{q}\} satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition (1.2).

For all T,ρ,δ>0T,\rho,\delta>0, there exists v∈L∞​((0,T),ℝq)v\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that ∥v∥L∞<ρ\lVert v\rVert_{L^{\infty}}<\rho, |x⁡(t,v)|<δ\lvert x(t;v)\rvert<\delta for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], and such that the end-point map

ℰT:{L∞​((0,T),ℝq)→ℝd,u↦x⁡(T,u)\mathcal{E}_{T}:\begin{cases}L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q})&\to\mathbb{R}^{d},\\ u&\mapsto x(T;u)\end{cases} (3.1)

has a surjective differential at vv, where x⁡(t,u)x(t;u) denotes the solution to (1.1) with initial condition x⁡(0)=0x(0)=0 and control uu.

3.1 Description of the induction mechanism

To prove Theorem 3.1, we proceed by induction on the number of distinct factors |Fac⁡(G)|≥0|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|\geq 0 involved in GG. The assumption that GG is factor-stable implies that

Fac+⁡(G)=Fac⁡(G)⊂G.\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(G)=\operatorname{Fac}(G)\subset G. (3.2)

The initialization is immediate.

Lemma 3.3.

For G⊂ℬgoodG\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} with |Fac⁡(G)|=0|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|=0, ΣG\Sigma_{G} is small-time globally controllable.

Proof.

Since Fac⁡(G)=∅\operatorname{Fac}(G)=\varnothing and X0∈ℬbadX_{0}\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, one has G⊂XgoodG\subset X_{\mathrm{good}}. Let T>0T>0, x∘,x∗∈ℝGx^{\circ},x^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{G}. For each Xi∈GX_{i}\in G, use the explicit constant control ui:=(xi∗−xi∘)/Tu_{i}:=(x^{*}_{i}-x^{\circ}_{i})/T, and ui=0u_{i}=0 when Xi∉GX_{i}\notin G. ∎

We now assume that Fac⁡(G)≠∅\operatorname{Fac}(G)\neq\varnothing. To perform the induction, we single out the largest factor of elements of GG, according to the underlying Hall order. We set

p:=max⁡Fac⁡(G)∈G.p:=\max\operatorname{Fac}(G)\in G. (3.3)

We partition GG as follows:

G=L⊔Z,whereZ:={b∈G∣p∈Fac⁡(b)}andL:=G∖Z.G=L\sqcup Z,\quad\text{where}\quad Z:=\{b\in G\mid p\in\operatorname{Fac}(b)\}\quad\text{and}\quad L:=G\setminus Z. (3.4)

The Hall order axioms entail the following elementary consequences.

Lemma 3.4.

One has:

  1. (i)

    for all b∈Zb\in Z, p<bp<b;

  2. (ii)

    p∈Lp\in L;

  3. (iii)

    Fac⁡(L)⊂L∩ℬ<p\operatorname{Fac}(L)\subset L\cap\mathcal{B}_{<p}.

Proof.

First, for b∈Zb\in Z, since p∈Fac⁡(b)p\in\operatorname{Fac}(b), Lemma 2.5 yields p<bp<b. Second, since p∈G=Z⊔Lp\in G=Z\sqcup L, p∈Lp\in L because p≮pp\not<p. Third, let ℓ∈L\ell\in L and a∈Fac⁡(ℓ)⊂Fac⁡(G)⊂Ga\in\operatorname{Fac}(\ell)\subset\operatorname{Fac}(G)\subset G. By (3.3), a≤pa\leq p. Moreover a≠pa\neq p (otherwise ℓ∈Z\ell\in Z by (3.4)). Thus a<pa<p and a∈ℬ<pa\in\mathcal{B}_{<p}. By (i), a∉Za\notin Z. So a∈La\in L. ∎

Corollary 3.5.

L⊂ℬgoodL\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} is factor-stable, Fac⁡(L)⊂Fac⁡(G)∖{p}\operatorname{Fac}(L)\subset\operatorname{Fac}(G)\setminus\{p\} and |Fac⁡(L)|<|Fac⁡(G)||\operatorname{Fac}(L)|<|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|.

The heart of the induction mechanism is the following result proved in Section 3.6.

Proposition 3.6.

Let κ≥1\kappa\geq 1. Assume that Theorem 3.1 holds for all sets satisfying |Fac⁡(G)|<κ|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|<\kappa. Let G⊂ℬgoodG\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} be finite, factor-stable, and such that |Fac⁡(G)|=κ|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|=\kappa. Then, for all T>0T>0,

{(ξb(T,u))b∈Z∣u∈L∞((0,T);ℝq) s.t., for all a∈G∖Z,ξa(T,u)=0}=ℝZ.\Big\{(\xi_{b}(T,u))_{b\in Z}\mid u\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q})\text{ s.t., for all }a\in G\setminus Z,\enskip\xi_{a}(T,u)=0\Big\}=\mathbb{R}^{Z}. (3.5)

Proposition 3.6 expresses that, for any T>0T>0, starting from the origin, one can find control loops reaching any desired target along the coordinates of ZZ at time TT, while driving the coordinates of LL back to 00. Once such loops are available, the induction follows easily.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

We proceed by induction on |Fac⁡(G)|≥0|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|\geq 0. The case |Fac⁡(G)|=0|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|=0 is covered in Lemma 3.3. Let κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, and assume that the result holds when |Fac⁡(G)|<κ|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|<\kappa.

Let G⊂ℬgoodG\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} with |Fac⁡(G)|=κ|\operatorname{Fac}(G)|=\kappa. We decompose the state x∈ℝG=ℝL×ℝZx\in\mathbb{R}^{G}=\mathbb{R}^{L}\times\mathbb{R}^{Z} as x=(xL,xZ)x=(x_{L},x_{Z}). Let T>0T>0, x∘,x∗∈ℝGx^{\circ},x^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{G}. By Corollary 3.5, we can apply the induction hypothesis to LL. Thus there exist controls u∘,u∗∈L∞​((0,T),ℝq)u^{\circ},u^{*}\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that

xL​(T,u∘,xL∘)=0LandxL​(T,u∗,0L)=xL∗.x_{L}(T;u^{\circ},x^{\circ}_{L})=0_{L}\quad\text{and}\quad x_{L}(T;u^{*},0_{L})=x^{*}_{L}. (3.6)

Given a control ul​o​o​p∈L∞​((0,T),ℝq)u^{loop}\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that xL​(T,ul​o​o​p,0L)=0Lx_{L}(T;u^{loop},0_{L})=0_{L}, define the concatenation u:=u∘⋄ul​o​o​p⋄u∗∈L∞​((0,3​T),ℝq)u:=u^{\circ}\diamond u^{loop}\diamond u^{*}\in L^{\infty}((0,3T);\mathbb{R}^{q}). The triangular nature of the system (2.16) and the concatenation property Lemma 2.23 imply that

xL​(3​T,u,xL∘)=xL∗andxZ​(3​T,u,x∘)=xZ​(T,u∘,x∘)+xZ​(T,ul​o​o​p,0)+xZ​(T,u∗,0).x_{L}(3T;u,x^{\circ}_{L})=x^{*}_{L}\quad\text{and}\quad x_{Z}(3T;u,x^{\circ})=x_{Z}(T;u^{\circ},x^{\circ})+x_{Z}(T;u^{loop},0)+x_{Z}(T;u^{*},0). (3.7)

By Proposition 3.6, there exists ul​o​o​p∈L∞​((0,T),ℝq)u^{loop}\in L^{\infty}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that xL​(T,ul​o​o​p,0L)=0Lx_{L}(T;u^{loop},0_{L})=0_{L} and

xZ​(T,ul​o​o​p,0)=xZ∗−xZ​(T,u∘,x∘)−xZ​(T,u∗,0).x_{Z}(T;u^{loop},0)=x^{*}_{Z}-x_{Z}(T;u^{\circ},x^{\circ})-x_{Z}(T;u^{*},0). (3.8)

We have thus found a control such that x⁡(3​T,u,x∘)=x∗x(3T;u,x^{\circ})=x^{*}, which proves the result by induction. ∎

3.2 Definition of the reduced system

We describe in this section a “reduced system” in which we use the coordinate associated with pp as a virtual control for the coordinates along ZZ. The reduced system is based on the following consequence of Definition 1.2 for elements of ZZ.

Definition 3.7.

Let b∈Zb\in Z. There exists a unique maximal mb≥1m_{b}\geq 1 and ρ⁡(b)∈ℬ\rho(b)\in\mathcal{B}, which we call the root of bb, such that b=adpmb⁡(ρ⁡(b))b=\ad_{p}^{m_{b}}(\rho(b)).

Lemma 3.8.

For all b∈Zb\in Z, one has p<ρ⁡(b)p<\rho(b), Fac⁡(ρ⁡(b))=Fac⁡(b)∖{p}={a∈Fac⁡(b)∣a<p}\operatorname{Fac}(\rho(b))=\operatorname{Fac}(b)\setminus\{p\}=\{a\in\operatorname{Fac}(b)\mid a<p\}. Finally Fac⁡(ρ⁡(b))⊂L∩ℬ<p\operatorname{Fac}(\rho(b))\subset L\cap\mathcal{B}_{<p}.

First, since b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B} and mb≥1m_{b}\geq 1, the inner bracket (p,ρ⁡(b))∈ℬ(p,\rho(b))\in\mathcal{B} so, p<ρ⁡(b)p<\rho(b) by the second Hall axiom. Second, the equality Fac⁡(ρ⁡(b))=Fac⁡(b)∖{p}\operatorname{Fac}(\rho(b))=\operatorname{Fac}(b)\setminus\{p\} follows from the full factorization (2.2) and the maximality of mbm_{b}. Third, by Lemma 2.5, all factors of ρ⁡(b)\rho(b) are strictly smaller than pp. Since they belong to GG, by (i) of Lemma 3.4, they belong to LL. ∎

Lemma 3.9.

Let b∈Zb\in Z. If ρ⁡(b)∈ℬbad\rho(b)\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, then mbm_{b} is odd.

Proof.

Write the full factorization (2.2) of bb. Since b∈Z⊂G⊂ℬgoodb\in Z\subset G\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}, all its factors are good. Thus all factors of ρ⁡(b)\rho(b) are good. By Definition 2.15, if ρ⁡(b)\rho(b) is bad, Xi=X0X_{i}=X_{0} and m1,…,mr−1m_{1},\dotsc,m_{r-1} are even. Since bb is good, mr=mbm_{r}=m_{b} is odd. ∎

The definition (2.11) of ξb\xi_{b} for b∈Zb\in Z yields:

ξ˙b=ξpmbmb!​ξ˙ρ⁡(b).\dot{\xi}_{b}=\frac{\xi_{p}^{m_{b}}}{m_{b}!}\dot{\xi}_{\rho(b)}. (3.9)

We will need to distinguish good and bad roots. We define the disjoint sets:

Rgood:=ρ⁡(Z)∩ℬgoodandRbad:=ρ⁡(Z)∩(ℬbad∖{X0}).R_{\mathrm{good}}:=\rho(Z)\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\quad\text{and}\quad R_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\rho(Z)\cap(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\setminus\{X_{0}\}). (3.10)

Thus Rgood∩Rbad=∅R_{\mathrm{good}}\cap R_{\mathrm{bad}}=\varnothing and Rgood⊔Rbad⊂ℬ∖{X0}R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}\subset\mathcal{B}\setminus\{X_{0}\} (we treat the possible root X0X_{0} on its own).

Y:={p}⊔Rgood,andC:=Y⊔Rbad={p}⊔Rgood⊔Rbad.Y:=\{p\}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{good}},\quad\text{and}\quad C:=Y\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{p\}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}. (3.11)

Lemma 3.10.

Proof.

Definition 3.11 (Reduced system).

Fix γ∈ℝRbad\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{\mathrm{bad}}}. We define the reduced system associated with GG and γ\gamma as the following system with states (y,z)∈ℝY×ℝZ(y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{Y}\times\mathbb{R}^{Z} and controls v∈ℝCv\in\mathbb{R}^{C}:

dd​t​(y,z)=F0​(yp)+∑c∈Cvc​Fc​(yp).\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}(y,z)=F_{0}(y_{p})+\sum_{c\in C}v_{c}F_{c}(y_{p}). (3.17)

We will need the following structural facts in the sequel.

Lemma 3.13.

One has Y∩ℬ<p=∅Y\cap\mathcal{B}_{<p}=\varnothing, Fac+⁡(C)⊂L∖Y\operatorname{Fac}^{+}(C)\subset L\setminus Y and L∖YL\setminus Y is factor-stable.

Proof.

First, since Y={p}⊔RgoodY=\{p\}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{good}}, Y∩ℬ<p=∅Y\cap\mathcal{B}_{<p}=\varnothing because p≮pp\not<p and p<cp<c for all c∈Rgoodc\in R_{\mathrm{good}} by Lemma 3.8.

3.3 Controllability of the reduced system

We investigate the controllability of the reduced system (3.17). We start with computations of the Lie brackets of the involved vector fields. Let 𝔏\mathfrak{L} denote the Lie algebra generated by the vector fields in (3.15) and (3.16).

The triangular structure of the vector fields VcV_{c} of (3.14) motivates the introduction of 𝒱\mathcal{V} as the space of polynomial vector fields which depend only on ypy_{p} and are supported in the zz directions. This is an abelian Lie algebra. Moreover, for all V∈𝒱V\in\mathcal{V},

[Fc,V]=0and[Fc,Fc′]=0, for all ​c,c′∈Rgood⊔Rbad⊔{X0}.[F_{c},V]=0\quad\text{and}\quad[F_{c},F_{c^{\prime}}]=0,\quad\text{ for all }c,c^{\prime}\in R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}\sqcup\{X_{0}\}. (3.18)

The only non-trivial brackets are those involving FpF_{p}.

Lemma 3.14.

For all c∈Rgood⊔Rbad⊔{X0}c\in R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}\sqcup\{X_{0}\} and m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N},

(∂ypmVc)​(0)={∂zb,if there exists b∈Z such that ​ρ​(b)=c​ and ​mb=m,0,otherwise.\bigl(\partial_{y_{p}}^{m}V_{c}\bigr)(0)=\begin{cases}\partial_{z_{b}},&\text{if there exists $b\in Z$ such that }\rho(b)=c\text{ and }m_{b}=m,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3.19)

In particular, the bracket bb in the first case is unique.

Proof.

By the definition of VcV_{c} and the factorial normalization,

(∂ypmVc)(0)=∑b∈Zρ⁡(b)=c𝟏{mb=m}∂zb.\bigl(\partial_{y_{p}}^{m}V_{c}\bigr)(0)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in Z\\ \rho(b)=c\end{subarray}}\mathbf{1}_{\{m_{b}=m\}}\partial_{z_{b}}. (3.20)

Moreover, the pair (ρ⁡(b),mb)(\rho(b),m_{b}) determines bb uniquely. ∎

Proposition 3.15.

For any γ∈ℝRbad\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{\mathrm{bad}}}, the reduced system (3.17) satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition at the origin, i.e. 𝔏⁡(0)=ℝY×ℝZ\mathfrak{L}(0)=\mathbb{R}^{Y}\times\mathbb{R}^{Z}.

Proof.

We obtain the different directions in successive steps.

  • •

    First, one has Fp(0)=∂ypF_{p}(0)=\partial_{y_{p}}. So ∂yp∈𝔏(0)\partial_{y_{p}}\in\mathfrak{L}(0).

  • •

    Second, for any b∈Zb\in Z, mb≥1m_{b}\geq 1, thus, for any c∈Rgood⊔Rbad⊔{X0}c\in R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}\sqcup\{X_{0}\}, Vc​(0)=0V_{c}(0)=0. Hence, for any a∈Rgooda\in R_{\mathrm{good}}, Fa(0)=∂yaF_{a}(0)=\partial_{y_{a}}. So ∂ya∈𝔏(0)\partial_{y_{a}}\in\mathfrak{L}(0) for all a∈Rgooda\in R_{\mathrm{good}}.

  • •

    Third, let b∈Zb\in Z with a root c:=ρ⁡(b)∈Rgood⊔Rbadc:=\rho(b)\in R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}} (not equal to X0X_{0}). Then adFpmb⁡(Fc)=∂ypmbVc\ad_{F_{p}}^{m_{b}}(F_{c})=\partial_{y_{p}}^{m_{b}}V_{c}, and Lemma 3.14 gives (∂ypmbVc)(0)=∂zb(\partial_{y_{p}}^{m_{b}}V_{c})(0)=\partial_{z_{b}}. Hence ∂zb∈𝔏(0)\partial_{z_{b}}\in\mathfrak{L}(0).

  • •

We can now prove the main result of this section.

Proposition 3.16.

For any γ∈ℝRbad\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{\mathrm{bad}}}, the reduced system (3.17) is L∞L^{\infty}-STLC at the origin.

Proof.

We plan to apply Sussmann’s theorem to the control-affine system (3.17). By Proposition 3.15, the Lie algebra rank condition at the origin is satisfied.

Let 𝒲:={F0}∪{Fc∣c∈Rgood⊔Rbad}\mathcal{W}:=\{F_{0}\}\cup\{F_{c}\mid c\in R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}\}. Any two elements of 𝒲\mathcal{W} commute. Moreover [𝒲,𝒱]=0[\mathcal{W},\mathcal{V}]=0 and, for any W∈𝒲W\in\mathcal{W}, [Fp,W]=∂ypW∈𝒱[F_{p},W]=\partial_{y_{p}}W\in\mathcal{V}.

Thus, the only potentially non-zero brackets are the adFpm⁡(Fc)\ad_{F_{p}}^{m}(F_{c}), for c∈Rgood⊔Rbad⊔{X0}c\in R_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup R_{\mathrm{bad}}\sqcup\{X_{0}\}. Among these, the only Sussmann-bad ones are the adFp2​m⁡(F0)=∂yp2​mF0\ad_{F_{p}}^{2m}(F_{0})=\partial_{y_{p}}^{2m}F_{0} for m≥0m\geq 0. By (3.15) and (3.14), the powers of ypy_{p} occurring in F0F_{0} are the ypmby_{p}^{m_{b}} for those b∈Zb\in Z whose root ρ⁡(b)\rho(b) is bad, and such mbm_{b} is odd by Lemma 3.9. So F0F_{0} is an odd function of ypy_{p}, hence so is ∂yp2​mF0\partial_{y_{p}}^{2m}F_{0}, which therefore vanishes at the origin.

Therefore, the conclusion follows from Theorem 1.9 (with any θ\theta). ∎

Keeping in mind that our goal is to prove Proposition 3.6, i.e. to control the components along ZZ while bringing the ones along other brackets back to 00, we will need the following continuous corollary. The continuous dependence on the target will be required in Section 3.6 to absorb the approximation errors which occur in the reduction process.

Corollary 3.17.

Let η>0\eta>0. There exists a neighborhood Θ\Theta of 00 in ℝZ\mathbb{R}^{Z} and a continuous map v:Θ→L∞​((0,1),ℝC)v:\Theta\to L^{\infty}((0,1);\mathbb{R}^{C}) such that, for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta,

  1. 1.

    the control vθv^{\theta} takes its values in [−η,η]C[-\eta,\eta]^{C};

  2. 2.

    the associated trajectory (yθ,zθ)(y^{\theta},z^{\theta}) remains in [−1,1]Y⊔Z[-1,1]^{Y\sqcup Z} for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1];

  3. 3.

    its final state is (yθ​(1),zθ​(1))=(0,θ)(y^{\theta}(1),z^{\theta}(1))=(0,\theta).

Proof.

By Proposition 3.15, the reduced system satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition. Thus, by Proposition 3.2, the reduced system has a normal trajectory in arbitrary state and control neighborhoods in time 12\frac{1}{2}. Let (y¯,z¯)(\bar{y},\bar{z}) be its endpoint. By Proposition 3.16, there is a control driving (y¯,z¯)(\bar{y},\bar{z}) to (0,0)(0,0) in time 12\frac{1}{2}. If the first trajectory is small, this correction remains in the prescribed neighborhoods. Normality is preserved, because the appended flow is a local diffeomorphism. The inverse function theorem then gives the result. ∎

3.4 Normal boxes around bad brackets

To perform the induction, we will also need to use bad brackets of RbadR_{\mathrm{bad}} as virtual controls. The difference with good brackets is that the available values for these brackets may not be centered at 00. Standard accessibility theory yields the following result.

Lemma 3.18 (Normal box).

Let H⊂ℬ∖{X0}H\subset\mathcal{B}\setminus\{X_{0}\} be finite and factor-stable. Set Hgood:=H∩ℬgoodH_{\mathrm{good}}:=H\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} and Hbad:=H∩ℬbadH_{\mathrm{bad}}:=H\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}. Assume that ΣHgood\Sigma_{H_{\mathrm{good}}} is small-time globally controllable. There exist γ∈ℝHbad\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{bad}}}, a neighborhood ΩH\Omega_{H} of 00 in ℝH\mathbb{R}^{H}, and a C1C^{1} map u¯:ΩH→L∞​((0,1),ℝq)\bar{u}:\Omega_{H}\to L^{\infty}((0,1);\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that, for all w∈ΩHw\in\Omega_{H},

∀b∈Hgood,\displaystyle\forall b\in H_{\mathrm{good}}, ξb​(1,u¯​[w])\displaystyle\qquad\xi_{b}(1,\bar{u}[w]) =wb,\displaystyle=w_{b}, (3.22)
∀b∈Hbad,\displaystyle\forall b\in H_{\mathrm{bad}}, ξb​(1,u¯​[w])\displaystyle\qquad\xi_{b}(1,\bar{u}[w]) =γb+wb.\displaystyle=\gamma_{b}+w_{b}. (3.23)
Proof.

By (2.17), ΣH\Sigma_{H} satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition. Apply Proposition 3.2 to ΣH\Sigma_{H} on the first half of the time interval. Let (xgood,xbad)(x_{\mathrm{good}},x_{\mathrm{bad}}) be the endpoint of the resulting normal control. Since both HH and ℬgood\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} are factor-stable, their intersection is too. Hence the subsystem indexed by HgoodH_{\mathrm{good}} is closed. On the second half of the interval, append a fixed control which drives xgoodx_{\mathrm{good}} back to 00. The endpoint of the full system is then of the form (0,γ)(0,\gamma).

The flow associated with the appended control is a local diffeomorphism. Hence the concatenated endpoint map is still submersive. Choose finitely many directions in L∞L^{\infty} on which its differential is an isomorphism. The inverse function theorem gives the conclusion. ∎

4 Proof of the necessary condition

We prove Theorem 1.7 by reducing it to the following purely algebraic “observability result”, which does not involve vector fields, or controls. The idea is that, under the conditions of Theorem 1.7, one can find an embedded system within (1.1) which is not L∞L^{\infty}-STLC. This embedded system is not STLC because one of its coordinates is ξb\xi_{b}, the coordinate of the second kind associated with the isolated bad bracket bb, which satisfies ξb​(t,u)≥0\xi_{b}(t,u)\geq 0.

Lemma 4.1.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a factor-parity Hall set on X=Xgood⊔XbadX=X_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup X_{\mathrm{bad}} where Xgood={X1,…,Xq}X_{\mathrm{good}}=\{X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\} and Xbad={X0}X_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{X_{0}\}. For any b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, T>0T>0, u∈L1​((0,T),ℝq)u\in L^{1}((0,T);\mathbb{R}^{q}) and t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T],

ξb​(t,u)≥0.\xi_{b}(t,u)\geq 0. (4.1)
Proof.

We prove by induction on |b||b| the stronger statement that ξ˙b​(⋅,u)≥0\dot{\xi}_{b}(\cdot,u)\geq 0 a.e. on (0,T)(0,T) for all b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}. Since ξb​(0,u)=0\xi_{b}(0,u)=0, this implies the desired conclusion.

For |b|=1|b|=1, one has b=X0b=X_{0}, hence ξ˙b=1\dot{\xi}_{b}=1. Let now b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} with |b|>1|b|>1, and write

b=adarmr​⋯​ada1m1⁡(seed⁡(b))so thatb=adam⁡(c)b=\ad_{a_{r}}^{m_{r}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(b))\quad\text{so that}\quad b=\ad_{a}^{m}(c) (4.2)

where a:=ara:=a_{r}, m:=mrm:=m_{r} and c:=adar−1mr−1​⋯​ada1m1⁡(seed⁡(b))c:=\ad_{a_{r-1}}^{m_{r-1}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(b)) (with c=seed⁡(b)c=\operatorname{seed}(b) when r=1r=1).

We claim that c∈ℬbadc\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} and that either a∈ℬbada\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} or mm is even. Indeed, if a∈ℬbada\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, then a<ca<c and ℬgood<ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, so necessarily c∈ℬbadc\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}. By (2.11),

By the induction hypothesis, ξ˙c≥0\dot{\xi}_{c}\geq 0 a.e. 4.1 Strategy for the proof of the observability result

We plan to prove Proposition 4.2 by induction on n:=|Fac∗⁡(b)|n:=\lvert\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\rvert, its statement being understood as universally quantified over all data (X,ℬ,K,b)(X,\mathcal{B},K,b). The case n=1n=1 is (4.5). In the induction step, one first discards the letters not occurring in bb (Lemma 4.5), so that p:=min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)p:=\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b) becomes the minimal letter of the alphabet, and is a good one (Section 4.2). Lazard elimination of pp then manufactures a new instance (Y,ℬY,KY,b^)(Y,\mathcal{B}_{Y},K_{Y},\hat{b}) of the same statement, with |FacY∗⁡(b^)|=n−1\lvert\operatorname{Fac}^{*}_{Y}(\hat{b})\rvert=n-1 (Lemma 4.6). Applying the induction hypothesis to it excludes Fac∗⁡(b)∖{p}\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\setminus\{p\} from suppℬ⁡(K∩Lie⁡(Y))\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}(K\cap\operatorname{Lie}(Y)). It remains to exclude pp itself: if some h∈Kh\in K had ⟨h,p⟩ℬ=1\langle h,p\rangle_{\mathcal{B}}=1, Proposition 4.3 below would produce c∈Fac∗⁡(b)∖{p}c\in\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\setminus\{p\} detected by Lie⁡({p}⊔(ℬbad∖{b}))\operatorname{Lie}(\{p\}\sqcup(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\setminus\{b\})), and substituting hh for pp would move that detection inside K∩Lie⁡(Y)K\cap\operatorname{Lie}(Y), a contradiction.

5 Proof of the support result

We prove Proposition 4.3. We need the following definition.

Definition 5.1 (Free associative algebra).

Let 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X) be the free associative ℝ\mathbb{R}-algebra on XX, in which we identify ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X) with the Lie subalgebra generated by XX for the commutator bracket. We equip 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X) with the scalar product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle for which the words in XX, including the empty word 𝟏\mathbf{1}, form an orthonormal basis. Each degX\deg_{X}-homogeneous component is then spanned by a finite set of words, so the components are finite-dimensional, pairwise orthogonal, and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle restricts to a scalar product on each of them; in particular ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is nondegenerate.

Throughout this section, ℬ\mathcal{B} is a factor-parity Hall set on X=Xgood⊔XbadX=X_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup X_{\mathrm{bad}}. We fix b∈ℬbad∖Xb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\setminus X such that Fac⁡(b)⊂ℬgood\operatorname{Fac}(b)\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}. We consider the following Lie subalgebra of ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X):

𝔥:=Lie⁡({p}⊔(ℬbad∖{b}))wherep:=min⁡Fac∗⁡(b)∈Xgood.\mathfrak{h}:=\operatorname{Lie}\left(\{p\}\sqcup(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\setminus\{b\})\right)\quad\text{where}\quad p:=\min\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\in X_{\mathrm{good}}. (5.1)

Let U⁡(𝔥)U(\mathfrak{h}) be the universal enveloping algebra of 𝔥\mathfrak{h}, which we identify with its image in 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X). In Section 5.1, we define a dual Hall coordinate Sb∈𝒜⁡(X)S_{b}\in\mathcal{A}(X). In Sections 5.3 and 5.2 we prove the following incompatible statements.

Proposition 5.2 (Detection).

There exists Z∈U⁡(𝔥)Z\in U(\mathfrak{h}) with ⟨Z,Sb⟩≠0\langle Z,S_{b}\rangle\neq 0.

Proposition 5.3 (Annihilation).

If suppℬ⁡(𝔥)∩(Fac∗⁡(b)∖{p})=∅\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathfrak{h})\cap(\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\setminus\{p\})=\varnothing, then ⟨⋅,Sb⟩=0\langle\cdot,S_{b}\rangle=0 on U⁡(𝔥)U(\mathfrak{h}).

Proof of Proposition 4.3.

Since the conclusions of Propositions 5.2 and 5.3 are incompatible, one has suppℬ⁡(𝔥)∩(Fac∗⁡(b)∖{p})≠∅\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathfrak{h})\cap(\operatorname{Fac}^{*}(b)\setminus\{p\})\neq\varnothing, which is exactly (4.7), the conclusion of Proposition 4.3. ∎

5.1 Dual Hall coordinates and residuals

5.1.1 Scalar product, coproduct and shuffle

We consider the tensor product 𝒜⁡(X)⊗𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X)\otimes\mathcal{A}(X) which we endow with (U⊗V)​(U′⊗V′):=U​U′⊗V​V′(U\otimes V)(U^{\prime}\otimes V^{\prime}):=UU^{\prime}\otimes VV^{\prime}, and with the scalar product for which the w⊗w′w\otimes w^{\prime} (for w,w′w,w^{\prime} words) form an orthonormal basis, so that ⟨U⊗V,U′⊗V′⟩=⟨U,U′⟩​⟨V,V′⟩\langle U\otimes V,U^{\prime}\otimes V^{\prime}\rangle=\langle U,U^{\prime}\rangle\langle V,V^{\prime}\rangle. Let Δ:𝒜⁡(X)→𝒜⁡(X)⊗𝒜⁡(X)\Delta:\mathcal{A}(X)\to\mathcal{A}(X)\otimes\mathcal{A}(X) be the unique algebra homomorphism such that Δ​y=y⊗𝟏+𝟏⊗y\Delta y=y\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes y for y∈Xy\in X. Every Lie element z∈ℒ⁡(X)z\in\mathcal{L}(X) is primitive (i.e. satisfies Δ​z=z⊗𝟏+𝟏⊗z\Delta z=z\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes z) by [16, Theorem 1.4].

For degX\deg_{X}-homogeneous F,G∈𝒜⁡(X)F,G\in\mathcal{A}(X), the linear form U↦⟨Δ​U,F⊗G⟩U\mapsto\langle\Delta U,F\otimes G\rangle vanishes on every degX\deg_{X}-homogeneous component except that of multidegree degX⁡F+degX⁡G\deg_{X}F+\deg_{X}G. By nondegeneracy, there is thus a unique F⊔⁣⊔G∈𝒜⁡(X)F\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}G\in\mathcal{A}(X), the shuffle of FF and GG, such that

⟨U,F⊔⁣⊔G⟩=⟨Δ​U,F⊗G⟩for all ​U∈𝒜⁡(X).\langle U,F\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}G\rangle=\langle\Delta U,F\otimes G\rangle\qquad\text{for all }U\in\mathcal{A}(X). (5.2)

The product ⊔⁣⊔\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup} is commutative and associative with unit 𝟏\mathbf{1} and degX⁡(F⊔⁣⊔G)=degX⁡F+degX⁡G\deg_{X}(F\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}G)=\deg_{X}F+\deg_{X}G for F,GF,G degX\deg_{X}-homogeneous. We then extend it by bilinearity.

5.1.2 PBW basis and its dual

A PBW-monomial is a product P=∏c∈ℬ↘cec​(P)P=\prod_{c\in\mathcal{B}}^{\searrow}c^{e_{c}(P)} taken in decreasing Hall order, where e⁡(P)∈ℕ(ℬ)e(P)\in\mathbb{N}^{(\mathcal{B})} has finite support. For PBW-monomials P,QP,Q, we write P⊙QP\odot Q for the PBW-monomial with e⁡(P⊙Q)=e⁡(P)+e⁡(Q)e(P\odot Q)=e(P)+e(Q). Since 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X) is the universal enveloping algebra of ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X) [16, Theorem 0.5], the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem asserts that the PBW-monomials form a basis of 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X). They are degX\deg_{X}-homogeneous, with degX⁡(P)=∑cec​(P)​degX⁡(c)\deg_{X}(P)=\sum_{c}e_{c}(P)\deg_{X}(c), so that, for each multidegree α∈ℕ(X)\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{(X)}, the finitely many PBW-monomials of multidegree α\alpha form a basis of this component of 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X).

Consequently, for every PBW-monomial PP there is a unique SP∈𝒜⁡(X)S_{P}\in\mathcal{A}(X) such that ⟨Q,SP⟩=δP,Q\langle Q,S_{P}\rangle=\delta_{P,Q} for every PBW-monomial QQ. It is degX\deg_{X}-homogeneous of multidegree degX⁡(P)\deg_{X}(P), S𝟏=𝟏S_{\mathbf{1}}=\mathbf{1}, and (SP)P(S_{P})_{P} is again a basis of 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X). We abbreviate ScS_{c} for c∈ℬc\in\mathcal{B}. Thus ⟨U,SP⟩\langle U,S_{P}\rangle is the coefficient of PP in the PBW expansion of U∈𝒜⁡(X)U\in\mathcal{A}(X). In particular, a Lie element expands on the one-term PBW-monomials only, whence

⟨z,c⟩ℬ=⟨z,Sc⟩for all ​z∈ℒ⁡(X),c∈ℬ.\langle z,c\rangle_{\mathcal{B}}=\langle z,S_{c}\rangle\qquad\text{for all }z\in\mathcal{L}(X),\ c\in\mathcal{B}. (5.3)

In other words, (SP)P(S_{P})_{P} is the bi-orthogonal family to the PBW-monomials for the scalar product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle on 𝒜⁡(X)\mathcal{A}(X). As an example, in a Hall set ℬ\mathcal{B} on X={X0,X1}X=\{X_{0},X_{1}\} for which X1<X0X_{1}<X_{0}, one has (X1,X0)∈ℬ(X_{1},X_{0})\in\mathcal{B} and

S(X1,X0)=X1​X0.S_{(X_{1},X_{0})}=X_{1}X_{0}. (5.4)

Indeed, for the one-term PBW-monomial (X1,X0)(X_{1},X_{0}) and the two-terms PBW monomial X0​X1X_{0}X_{1},

⟨[X1,X0],S(X1,X0)⟩=⟨X1​X0−X0​X1,X1​X0⟩=1and⟨X0​X1,S(X1,X0)⟩=0.\langle[X_{1},X_{0}],S_{(X_{1},X_{0})}\rangle=\langle X_{1}X_{0}-X_{0}X_{1},X_{1}X_{0}\rangle=1\quad\text{and}\quad\langle X_{0}X_{1},S_{(X_{1},X_{0})}\rangle=0. (5.5)

We now recall two properties of the basis dual to the PBW basis associated with a Hall set; see [16, Theorem 5.3]. Since [16] uses a different Hall set convention, we provide a proof in Appendix B.

Lemma 5.4.

For PBW-monomials P,QP,Q,

SP⊔⁣⊔SQ=(∏c∈ℬ(ec​(P)+ec​(Q)ec​(P)))​SP⊙Q,henceSP=⊔⁣⊔c∈ℬ⁡Sc⊔⁣⊔ec​(P)ec​(P)!.S_{P}\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}S_{Q}=\Bigl(\prod_{c\in\mathcal{B}}\binom{e_{c}(P)+e_{c}(Q)}{e_{c}(P)}\Bigr)S_{P\odot Q},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad S_{P}=\mathop{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}}_{c\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{S_{c}^{\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}e_{c}(P)}}{e_{c}(P)!}. (5.6)

5.1.3 Residuals

For y∈Xy\in X, the residuals ℓy,ry:𝒜⁡(X)→𝒜⁡(X)\ell_{y},r_{y}:\mathcal{A}(X)\to\mathcal{A}(X) are the linear maps defined on words by ℓy​(y​w)=w\ell_{y}(yw)=w, ry​(w​y)=wr_{y}(wy)=w, and by 00 on words not having the indicated first (resp. last) letter. Lemma 5.6.

Let y∈Xy\in X, a∈ℒ⁡(X)a\in\mathcal{L}(X), F,G,U,V∈𝒜⁡(X)F,G,U,V\in\mathcal{A}(X) and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Then

⟨y​U,F⟩=⟨U,ℓy​F⟩,⟨U​y,F⟩=⟨U,ry​F⟩;\displaystyle\langle yU,F\rangle=\langle U,\ell_{y}F\rangle,\quad\langle Uy,F\rangle=\langle U,r_{y}F\rangle; (5.9)
∂y=ℓyand⟨Dyn(U),F⟩=⟨U,(ℓy−ry)nF⟩;\displaystyle\partial_{y}=\ell_{y}\quad\text{and}\quad\langle D_{y}^{n}(U),F\rangle=\langle U,(\ell_{y}-r_{y})^{n}F\rangle; (5.10)

∂a(F​y)=(∂aF)​yif a and F are deg-homogeneous with ​deg⁡F≥deg⁡a,\displaystyle\partial_{a}(Fy)=(\partial_{a}F)y\quad\text{if $a$ and $F$ are $\deg$-homogeneous with }\deg F\geq\deg a, (5.13)

Proof.

The two identities (5.9) are read off the definitions on words. (5.11) is likewise immediate on words. By (5.8) and (5.9), ∂y=ℓy\partial_{y}=\ell_{y} and ℓy−ry\ell_{y}-r_{y} is the adjoint of DyD_{y}, whence (5.10), the adjoint of DynD_{y}^{n} being the nn-th power of the adjoint of DyD_{y}.

For (5.12), let U∈𝒜⁡(X)U\in\mathcal{A}(X). Since Δ\Delta is a homomorphism and aa is primitive, (5.8) and (5.2) give

⟨U,∂a(F⊔⁣⊔G)⟩=⟨Δ⁡(a​U),F⊗G⟩=⟨(a⊗𝟏+𝟏⊗a)​Δ​U,F⊗G⟩=⟨Δ​U,(∂aF)⊗G+F⊗(∂aG)⟩,\begin{split}\langle U,\partial_{a}(F\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}G)\rangle=\langle\Delta(aU),F\otimes G\rangle&=\langle(a\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes a)\Delta U,F\otimes G\rangle\\ &=\langle\Delta U,(\partial_{a}F)\otimes G+F\otimes(\partial_{a}G)\rangle,\end{split} (5.14)

using (5.8) on each tensor factor. By (5.2) again, this is ⟨U,(∂aF)⊔⁣⊔G+F⊔⁣⊔(∂aG)⟩\langle U,(\partial_{a}F)\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}G+F\mathbin{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(\partial_{a}G)\rangle.

Appendix A Comparison with classical sufficient conditions

We first show that, in our sufficient condition, only the bad brackets having no bad factor need to be compensated. We then compare this irreducible family with the bad brackets occurring in the conditions of Sussmann, Agrachev–Gamkrelidze and Krastanov.

Throughout the appendix, Xgood={X1,…,Xq}X_{\mathrm{good}}=\{X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\}, Xbad={X0}X_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{X_{0}\} and ℬ=ℬgood⊔ℬbad\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} is a factor-parity Hall set on XX. We recall the family of Sussmann-bad brackets

Sbad:={b∈Br⁡(X)∣n0​(b)​ is odd and ​ni​(b)​ is even for ​1≤i≤q}.S_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\left\{b\in\Br(X)\mid n_{0}(b)\text{ is odd and }n_{i}(b)\text{ is even for }1\leq i\leq q\right\}. (A.1)

A.1 Parity of bad brackets

All the parity properties we need follow from the following lemma, which we state over an arbitrary alphabet since we will also apply it after Lazard elimination.

Lemma A.1 (Parity).

Let ℋ=ℋgood⊔ℋbad\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}} be a factor-parity Hall set on an alphabet Y=Ygood⊔YbadY=Y_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup Y_{\mathrm{bad}} and let b∈ℋbadb\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}, with factorization b=adarmr​⋯​ada1m1⁡(seed⁡(b))b=\ad_{a_{r}}^{m_{r}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(b)). Then

  1. (i)

    seed⁡(b)∈Ybad\operatorname{seed}(b)\in Y_{\mathrm{bad}}, and mjm_{j} is even for every good factor aja_{j};

  2. (ii)

    ny​(b)n_{y}(b) is even for every y∈Ygoody\in Y_{\mathrm{good}};

  3. (iii)

    if moreover Fac⁡(b)⊂ℋgood\operatorname{Fac}(b)\subset\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{good}}, then every mjm_{j} is even and ∑y∈Ybadny​(b)\sum_{y\in Y_{\mathrm{bad}}}n_{y}(b) is odd.

Proof.

c:=adak−1mk−1​⋯​ada1m1⁡(seed⁡(b))∈ℋ.c:=\ad_{a_{k-1}}^{m_{k-1}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(b))\in\mathcal{H}. (A.2)

Then c∈ℋbadc\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}: either c=bc=b, or ak<ca_{k}<c by the second Hall axiom and ℋgood<ℋbad\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}. All the factors of cc are good, so (2.9) applied to cc yields seed⁡(b)=seed⁡(c)∈Ybad\operatorname{seed}(b)=\operatorname{seed}(c)\in Y_{\mathrm{bad}} and m1,…,mk−1m_{1},\dotsc,m_{k-1} even. Since ℋgood<ℋbad\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}, the brackets a1,…,ak−1a_{1},\dotsc,a_{k-1} are exactly the good factors of bb.

(ii) Induction on |b|\lvert b\rvert, using ny​(b)=ny​(seed⁡(b))+∑jmj​ny​(aj)n_{y}(b)=n_{y}(\operatorname{seed}(b))+\sum_{j}m_{j}n_{y}(a_{j}): by (i) the seed contributes nothing, the good factors occur with even multiplicity, and each bad factor contains an even number of occurrences of yy by the induction hypothesis.

(iii) Here k=r+1k=r+1, so all the mjm_{j} are even by (i). Writing σ⁡(a):=∑y∈Ybadny​(a)\sigma(a):=\sum_{y\in Y_{\mathrm{bad}}}n_{y}(a), one gets σ⁡(b)=1+∑jmj​σ​(aj)\sigma(b)=1+\sum_{j}m_{j}\sigma(a_{j}), which is odd. ∎

Specialized to Xbad={X0}X_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{X_{0}\}, items (ii) and (iii) read as follows.

Corollary A.2.

If b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} satisfies Fac⁡(b)⊂ℬgood\operatorname{Fac}(b)\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}, then b∈Sbadb\in S_{\mathrm{bad}}.

A.2 Irreducible bad brackets

We define the set of irreducible bad brackets as

ℬbadirr:=ℬbad∖(ℬbad,ℬbad).\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}:=\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\setminus(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}},\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}). (A.3)
Lemma A.3.

Every b∈ℬbadirrb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}} satisfies Fac⁡(b)⊂ℬgood\operatorname{Fac}(b)\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}.

Proof.

Write b=adarmr​⋯​ada1m1⁡(seed⁡(b))b=\ad_{a_{r}}^{m_{r}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(b)) and assume that some factor is bad; then so is ara_{r}, since a1<⋯<ara_{1}<\dotsb<a_{r} and ℬgood<ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}<\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}. Set c:=adarmr−1​adar−1mr−1​⋯​ada1m1⁡(seed⁡(b))∈ℬc:=\ad_{a_{r}}^{m_{r}-1}\ad_{a_{r-1}}^{m_{r-1}}\dotsb\ad_{a_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(b))\in\mathcal{B}. The second Hall axiom gives ar<ca_{r}<c, hence c∈ℬbadc\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} and b=(ar,c)∈(ℬbad,ℬbad)b=(a_{r},c)\in(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}},\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}), a contradiction. ∎

We now show that the reducible bad brackets of (ℬbad,ℬbad)(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}},\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}) do not have to be compensated separately. Fix now θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), recall the weight ωθ​(b)=θ​n0​(b)+n1​(b)+⋯+nq​(b)\omega_{\theta}(b)=\theta n_{0}(b)+n_{1}(b)+\dotsb+n_{q}(b) and set, for r>0r>0,

ℒ<r\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{<r} :=span⁡{a∈ℬ∣ωθ​(a)<r},\displaystyle:=\vect\{a\in\mathcal{B}\mid\omega_{\theta}(a)<r\}, (A.4)
ℒ≤r\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\leq r} :=span⁡{a∈ℬ∣ωθ​(a)≤r},\displaystyle:=\vect\{a\in\mathcal{B}\mid\omega_{\theta}(a)\leq r\}, (A.5)
𝒢<r\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{<r} :=span⁡{a∈ℬgood∣ωθ​(a)<r}.\displaystyle:=\vect\{a\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}\mid\omega_{\theta}(a)<r\}. (A.6)

Since ωθ\omega_{\theta} is additive with respect to the multidegree, the Hall expansion of a bracket preserves the weight, so that

[ℒ≤r,ℒ<s]⊂ℒ<r+s.[\mathcal{L}_{\leq r},\mathcal{L}_{<s}]\subset\mathcal{L}_{<r+s}. (A.7)

Finally, for a control-affine system (1.1), let

Kf:={z∈ℒ⁡(X)∣fz​(0)=0},K_{f}:=\{z\in\mathcal{L}(X)\mid f_{z}(0)=0\}, (A.8)

which is a Lie subalgebra of ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}(X), as already used in the proof of Theorem 1.7.

For b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, our compensation condition (1.6) reads

b∈Kf+𝒢<ωθ​(b),b\in K_{f}+\mathcal{G}_{<\omega_{\theta}(b)}, (A.9)

while Sussmann’s condition of Theorem 1.9 reads

∀b∈Sbad,b∈Kf+ℒ<ωθ​(b).\forall b\in S_{\mathrm{bad}},\qquad b\in K_{f}+\mathcal{L}_{<\omega_{\theta}(b)}. (A.10)

The next lemma contains both comparisons: it upgrades a compensation of only the irreducible bad brackets by arbitrary brackets of lower weight into a compensation of all bad brackets by good brackets of lower weight.

Lemma A.4 (Absorption).

Let θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and assume that b∈Kf+ℒ<ωθ​(b)b\in K_{f}+\mathcal{L}_{<\omega_{\theta}(b)} for every b∈ℬbadirrb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}. Then b∈Kf+𝒢<ωθ​(b)b\in K_{f}+\mathcal{G}_{<\omega_{\theta}(b)} for every b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}.

Proof.

Assume by contradiction that some bad bracket fails (A.9) and choose one, say bb, of minimal weight ω:=ωθ​(b)\omega:=\omega_{\theta}(b). Such a choice is possible because ωθ​(a)≥θ​|a|\omega_{\theta}(a)\geq\theta\lvert a\rvert, so that only finitely many brackets have weight below a given bound. We claim that, in any case,

b∈Kf+ℒ<ω.b\in K_{f}+\mathcal{L}_{<\omega}. (A.11)

If b∈ℬbadirrb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}, this is the assumption. Otherwise b=(a,c)b=(a,c) with a,c∈ℬbada,c\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}, and ωθ​(a),ωθ​(c)<ω\omega_{\theta}(a),\omega_{\theta}(c)<\omega by positivity and additivity of the weight. By minimality of bb, one can write a=ka+gaa=k_{a}+g_{a} and c=kc+gcc=k_{c}+g_{c} with ka,kc∈Kfk_{a},k_{c}\in K_{f}, ga∈𝒢<ωθ​(a)g_{a}\in\mathcal{G}_{<\omega_{\theta}(a)} and gc∈𝒢<ωθ​(c)g_{c}\in\mathcal{G}_{<\omega_{\theta}(c)}. In particular ka∈ℒ≤ωθ​(a)k_{a}\in\mathcal{L}_{\leq\omega_{\theta}(a)} and kc∈ℒ≤ωθ​(c)k_{c}\in\mathcal{L}_{\leq\omega_{\theta}(c)}. Hence

b=[a,c]=[ka,kc]+([ka,gc]+[ga,kc]+[ga,gc]),b=[a,c]=[k_{a},k_{c}]+\bigl([k_{a},g_{c}]+[g_{a},k_{c}]+[g_{a},g_{c}]\bigr), (A.12)

where [ka,kc]∈Kf[k_{a},k_{c}]\in K_{f} since KfK_{f} is a Lie subalgebra, while the parenthesis lies in ℒ<ω\mathcal{L}_{<\omega} by (A.7). This proves (A.11).

Expand now in the Hall basis the component of bb lying in ℒ<ω\mathcal{L}_{<\omega}. Its good terms belong to 𝒢<ω\mathcal{G}_{<\omega}, and each of its bad terms dd satisfies ωθ​(d)<ω\omega_{\theta}(d)<\omega, hence d∈Kf+𝒢<ωθ​(d)⊂Kf+𝒢<ωd\in K_{f}+\mathcal{G}_{<\omega_{\theta}(d)}\subset K_{f}+\mathcal{G}_{<\omega} by minimality of bb. Therefore b∈Kf+𝒢<ωb\in K_{f}+\mathcal{G}_{<\omega}, a contradiction. ∎

Proposition A.5 (Compensation of irreducible bad brackets).

Let θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1). Then (A.9) holds for every b∈ℬbadb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}} if and only if it holds for every b∈ℬbadirrb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}.

Proof.

The converse implication follows from Lemma A.4 and 𝒢<r⊂ℒ<r\mathcal{G}_{<r}\subset\mathcal{L}_{<r}. ∎

Thus the family of bad brackets requiring direct compensation in our sufficient condition is ℬbadirr\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}, not the whole of ℬbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}: reducible bad brackets are obtained by bracketing two smaller bad brackets, and their compensation follows recursively from the fact that KfK_{f} is a Lie subalgebra.

A.3 Sussmann’s bad brackets

It is not true that ℬbad⊂Sbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\subset S_{\mathrm{bad}}: bracketing two bad brackets need not preserve the parity of n0n_{0}. By Lemmas A.3 and A.2, however, all the bad brackets requiring direct compensation ℬbadirr\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}} do belong to SbadS_{\mathrm{bad}}, which yields the following comparison.

Corollary A.6.

If a system (1.1) satisfies (A.10) for some θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), then it satisfies (1.6) for the same θ\theta. Hence Theorem 1.8 applies to every system to which Theorem 1.9 applies.

Proof.

By Lemmas A.3 and A.2, ℬbadirr⊂Sbad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}\subset S_{\mathrm{bad}}, so (A.10) provides the assumption of Lemma A.4. ∎

A.4 Agrachev–Gamkrelidze and Krastanov filters

Both the Agrachev–Gamkrelidze sufficient condition of [1] and the Krastanov sufficient condition of [15] start from a given set Π\Pi satisfying some properties. A natural way to construct this set Π\Pi is to obtain it by Lazard elimination, as done by the authors in their examples. The purpose of this paragraph is to compare, when Π\Pi is obtained in that way, the sets of brackets considered as bad by Agrachev–Gamkrelidze AGbad\mathrm{AG}_{\mathrm{bad}}, by Krastanov Kbad\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{bad}} and by a factor-parity Hall set ℬbadirr\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}. We do not claim that our Theorem 1.8 implies theirs for two different reasons:

  • •

    Although not illustrated by examples, their theorems allow more general sets Π\Pi.

  • •

    Their compensation condition uses a more general weight than the Sussmann weight of (1.5).

Recall that ℬ\mathcal{B} denotes a factor-parity Hall set on XX with Xgood={X1,…,Xq}X_{\mathrm{good}}=\{X_{1},\dotsc,X_{q}\} and Xbad={X0}X_{\mathrm{bad}}=\{X_{0}\}. Let Π\Pi be an alphabet obtained from (X,ℬ)(X,\mathcal{B}) by successive Hall-compatible Lazard eliminations, and let E⊂ℬE\subset\mathcal{B} be the set of eliminated Hall elements. In other words, EE is an initial segment of ℬ\mathcal{B}. We assume (as in [1, 15]) that

Sbad⊂Lie⁡(Π).S_{\mathrm{bad}}\subset\operatorname{Lie}(\Pi). (A.13)

Repeated application of Lemma 4.6 shows that EE is factor-stable, that Fac⁡(Π)⊂E\operatorname{Fac}(\Pi)\subset E, and that the Hall set induced on Π\Pi is again of the factor-parity class (so Π=Πgood⊔Πbad\Pi=\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\sqcup\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}), the good/bad status of every non-eliminated Hall element being preserved. We identify this final Hall set with ℬ∖E\mathcal{B}\setminus E. For b∈ℬ∖Eb\in\mathcal{B}\setminus E, we denote by degΠ⁡(b)\deg_{\Pi}(b) its total degree over Π\Pi and by nπ​(b)n_{\pi}(b) the multiplicity of the letter π∈Π\pi\in\Pi in its expression over Π\Pi. Since Lie⁡(Π)\operatorname{Lie}(\Pi) is spanned by e​(ℬ∖E)\textnormal{{e}}(\mathcal{B}\setminus E), an eliminated Hall element cannot lie in Lie⁡(Π)\operatorname{Lie}(\Pi), so (A.13) forces

E∩Sbad=∅.E\cap S_{\mathrm{bad}}=\varnothing. (A.14)

The definitions of the bad brackets to be compensated in [1, 15] are as follows:

AGbad⁡(Π)\displaystyle\operatorname{AG}_{\mathrm{bad}}(\Pi) :={b∈(ℬ∖E)∩Sbad|degΠ⁡(b)​ is odd},\displaystyle:=\left\{b\in(\mathcal{B}\setminus E)\cap S_{\mathrm{bad}}\;\middle|\;\deg_{\Pi}(b)\text{ is odd}\right\}, (A.15)
Kbad⁡(Π)\displaystyle\operatorname{K}_{\mathrm{bad}}(\Pi) :={b∈AGbad⁡(Π)|nπ​(b)​ is even for every ​π∈Π∖Sbad}.\displaystyle:=\left\{b\in\operatorname{AG}_{\mathrm{bad}}(\Pi)\;\middle|\;n_{\pi}(b)\text{ is even for every }\pi\in\Pi\setminus S_{\mathrm{bad}}\right\}. (A.16)
Lemma A.7.

One has E⊂ℬgoodE\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}} and Πbad⊂Sbad\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}\subset S_{\mathrm{bad}}. In particular Π∖Sbad⊂Πgood\Pi\setminus S_{\mathrm{bad}}\subset\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}.

Proof.

If E∩ℬbad≠∅E\cap\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}\neq\varnothing, pick ee in it of minimal length. Since EE is factor-stable, Fac⁡(e)⊂E\operatorname{Fac}(e)\subset E, so no factor of ee is bad, by minimality of |e|\lvert e\rvert. Hence e∈Sbade\in S_{\mathrm{bad}} by Corollary A.2, contradicting (A.14). Thus E⊂ℬgoodE\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}. Let now π∈Πbad\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}: then Fac⁡(π)⊂E⊂ℬgood\operatorname{Fac}(\pi)\subset E\subset\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{good}}, so π∈Sbad\pi\in S_{\mathrm{bad}}, again by Corollary A.2. ∎

Proposition A.8.

Under the assumptions above,

ℬbadirr⊂Kbad⁡(Π)⊂AGbad⁡(Π)⊂Sbad.\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}\subset\operatorname{K}_{\mathrm{bad}}(\Pi)\subset\operatorname{AG}_{\mathrm{bad}}(\Pi)\subset S_{\mathrm{bad}}. (A.17)
Proof.

The last two inclusions are immediate from (A.15)–(A.16). Let b∈ℬbadirrb\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{bad}}^{\mathrm{irr}}. By Lemma A.3, b∈Sbadb\in S_{\mathrm{bad}}, hence b∉Eb\notin E by (A.14), so bb is a bad Hall bracket over Π\Pi. Applying Lemma A.1 (ii) to the factor-parity Hall set on Π\Pi and using Lemma A.7,

nπ​(b)≡0(mod2)for every ​π∈Πgood⊃Π∖Sbad,n_{\pi}(b)\equiv 0\pmod{2}\qquad\text{for every }\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\supset\Pi\setminus S_{\mathrm{bad}}, (A.18)

which is the parity condition of (A.16). Moreover, by additivity of the XX-multidegree under substitution of the generators,

n0​(b)=∑π∈Πnπ​(b)​n0​(π)≡∑π∈Πbadnπ​(b)≡∑π∈Πnπ​(b)=degΠ⁡(b)(mod2),n_{0}(b)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi}n_{\pi}(b)n_{0}(\pi)\equiv\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}}n_{\pi}(b)\equiv\sum_{\pi\in\Pi}n_{\pi}(b)=\deg_{\Pi}(b)\pmod{2}, (A.19)

the two congruences following from (A.18), together with the oddness of n0​(π)n_{0}(\pi) for π∈Πbad⊂Sbad\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{bad}}\subset S_{\mathrm{bad}}. Since b∈Sbadb\in S_{\mathrm{bad}}, n0​(b)n_{0}(b) is odd, hence so is degΠ⁡(b)\deg_{\Pi}(b) and b∈Kbad⁡(Π)b\in\operatorname{K}_{\mathrm{bad}}(\Pi). ∎

To summarize, Sussmann’s symmetry argument singles out the parity set SbadS_{\mathrm{bad}}. Agrachev–Gamkrelidze first change the free generating family, then retain the elements of odd total degree in the new generators. Krastanov retains in addition the parity of each individual generator outside the Sussmann set. Factor-parity Hall sets make the same mechanism recursive: once a good generator has been eliminated, the induced alphabet is again split into good and bad generators, and the parity rule is applied anew.

Appendix B PBW triangularity and the dual Hall factorization

B.1 PBW triangularity

Lemma B.1 (PBW triangularity).

Let D=d1⋯dkD=d_{1}\cdots d_{k} be a decreasing PBW-monomial and let e1,…,eℓ∈ℬe_{1},\dots,e_{\ell}\in\mathcal{B}. Assume that, for some t≤min⁡(k,ℓ)t\leq\min(k,\ell), et>dte_{t}>d_{t} and ej=dje_{j}=d_{j} for all j<tj<t. Then every PBW-monomial occurring in the PBW expansion of e1⋯eℓe_{1}\cdots e_{\ell} is strictly larger than DD.

Proof.

We argue lexicographically on ℓ\ell and the number of inversions of the sequence e1,…,eℓe_{1},\dots,e_{\ell}. If the sequence is decreasing, then for every c>etc>e_{t} the multiplicities of cc in DD and in e1⋯eℓe_{1}\cdots e_{\ell} agree, while the latter has strictly larger multiplicity at ete_{t}. Hence D≺e1⋯eℓD\prec e_{1}\cdots e_{\ell} by the definition of the PBW order. Otherwise choose ii with ei<ei+1e_{i}<e_{i+1}. Straightening this adjacent inversion gives

e1⋯eℓ=e1⋯ei+1ei⋯eℓ+∑c∈suppℬ⁡[ei,ei+1]λce1⋯ei−1cei+2⋯eℓ.e_{1}\cdots e_{\ell}=e_{1}\cdots e_{i+1}e_{i}\cdots e_{\ell}+\sum_{c\in\operatorname{supp}_{\mathcal{B}}[e_{i},e_{i+1}]}\lambda_{c}\,e_{1}\cdots e_{i-1}c\,e_{i+2}\cdots e_{\ell}. (B.1)

Every occurring cc satisfies c>eic>e_{i} by Lemma 2.9 and the third Hall axiom. The first term has one fewer inversion, while every term in the sum has one fewer term. It remains only to check that the hypothesis is preserved. One cannot have i≤t−2i\leq t-2, since ei=di≥di+1=ei+1e_{i}=d_{i}\geq d_{i+1}=e_{i+1} there. If i=t−1i=t-1, both kinds of terms have their first strict increase over DD already at position t−1t-1. If i=ti=t, they have it at position tt. If i≥t+1i\geq t+1, their first tt factors are unchanged. The induction hypothesis therefore applies to every term. ∎

B.2 Dual of a PBW-monomial

Proof of Lemma 5.4.

For c∈ℬc\in\mathcal{B}, Δ​c=c⊗𝟏+𝟏⊗c\Delta c=c\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes c, and c⊗𝟏c\otimes\mathbf{1} commutes with 𝟏⊗c\mathbf{1}\otimes c. Hence, for a PBW-monomial RR,

Δ​R=∏c∈ℬ↘(c⊗𝟏+𝟏⊗c)ec​(R)=∑A⊙B=R(∏c∈ℬ(ec​(R)ec​(A)))​A⊗B,\Delta R=\prod_{c\in\mathcal{B}}^{\searrow}\bigl(c\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes c\bigr)^{e_{c}(R)}=\sum_{A\odot B=R}\Bigl(\prod_{c\in\mathcal{B}}\binom{e_{c}(R)}{e_{c}(A)}\Bigr)A\otimes B, (B.2)

the sum being over pairs of PBW-monomials with e⁡(A)+e⁡(B)=e⁡(R)e(A)+e(B)=e(R). Taking the scalar product with SP⊗SQS_{P}\otimes S_{Q} and using (5.2) gives the first identity. The second follows by iteration. ∎

Lemma B.2 (Terminal contraction).

Py=p1⋯pidi+1+Ri,Py=p_{1}\cdots p_{i}\,d_{i+1}+R_{i}, (B.4)

where every PBW-monomial occurring in RiR_{i} has at least two factors. For i=mi=m, this holds with Rm=0R_{m}=0. Assume (B.4) for some i≥1i\geq 1. In straightening p1⋯pidi+1p_{1}\cdots p_{i}d_{i+1}, the final factor di+1d_{i+1} is never involved: straightening two preceding factors either interchanges them or replaces them by a Hall element larger than the smaller one, hence still at least di+1d_{i+1}. Lemma B.3 (Recognition).

Let c∈ℬ∖Xc\in\mathcal{B}\setminus X and write its factorization as c=adcrmr​⋯​adc1m1⁡(seed⁡(c))c=\ad_{c_{r}}^{m_{r}}\dotsb\ad_{c_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\operatorname{seed}(c)). Set Mc:=crmr⋯c1m1M_{c}:=c_{r}^{m_{r}}\cdots c_{1}^{m_{1}}. Then, for every PBW-monomial PP and every y∈Xy\in X,

the last inequality by the third Hall axiom. This is the Hall factorization of cc, so uniqueness in Lemma 2.4 gives P=McP=M_{c} and y=seed⁡(c)y=\operatorname{seed}(c). Proof of Lemma 5.5.

Let c∈ℬ∖Xc\in\mathcal{B}\setminus X and McM_{c} be as above. For every word uu and every y∈Xy\in X, expanding u=∑P⟨u,SP⟩​Pu=\sum_{P}\langle u,S_{P}\rangle P, and using Lemma B.3, we obtain

⟨u​y,Sc⟩=∑P⟨u,SP⟩​⟨P​y,Sc⟩=δy,seed⁡(c)​⟨u,SMc⟩=⟨u​y,SMc​seed⁡(c)⟩.\langle uy,S_{c}\rangle=\sum_{P}\langle u,S_{P}\rangle\langle Py,S_{c}\rangle=\delta_{y,\operatorname{seed}(c)}\langle u,S_{M_{c}}\rangle=\langle uy,S_{M_{c}}\operatorname{seed}(c)\rangle. (B.8)

Every word of degree |c|≥2\lvert c\rvert\geq 2 is of the form u​yuy, and ScS_{c} and SMc​seed⁡(c)S_{M_{c}}\operatorname{seed}(c) are deg\deg-homogeneous of that degree. Hence Sc=SMc​seed⁡(c)S_{c}=S_{M_{c}}\operatorname{seed}(c). ∎
